Reproduced here are 78 of the 349 letters of the Servant of God found so far.

The collection covers a span of about 12/15 years of her life, including also the undated ones. For these last, an attempt has been made to give an indirect placement, through analysis of the content, the evolution of her handwriting, the paper used, and the external circumstances.

Some can be dated with certainty to the years 1872-1875.

The first dated letter dates back to March 1873; the last is from 28 May 1885, 10 days before her death; and although not a few letters have been lost, the collection is nonetheless fairly rich in the number of letters and in content.

Of the 349 letters:

326 are addressed to the Foundress, Mother Rosa Gattorno,

17 to some fellow Daughters of St. Anne,

6 to others.

Spread over the period already indicated, the letters reflect in particular the last period of the Servant of God's life, sketch out something of Sister Anna del Salvatore's character, and let us know what she thinks, the ideals dear to her, the experiences she lives through, and her peculiar way of moving and acting within the ordinariness of the life and mission she carries out.

As to their composition, they reveal the Servant of God's scant schooling - though gifted with spontaneity and immediacy - to which must be added the haste with which she writes, her little care in completing sentences, the simplicity of her expression, the difficulty of conveying what she wishes or what she is asking advice about, her asking forgiveness for unintended distractions, or for having caused displeasure or suffering through her behavior. Always, in every letter, between the lines, one perceives an acknowledgment of her unworthiness, constantly confessed.

Rich in delicacy and humility, the Servant of God often questions herself about her strength and her ways of acting in the responsibilities entrusted to her, always declaring herself ready for obedience and sincerely willing to accept any observation or help.

From her clear, frank, straightforward expressions there emerges a deep love for the Lord and the desire to make Him loved through simplicity of life, zeal in works, perseverance in self-giving, and the daily freshness of her offering.

As for the present edition, an effort has been made to remain as faithful as possible to the original wording, with only a few essential orthographic touch-ups, adding in square brackets the most plausible location and dating.

In the selection made here, the following order has been followed:

a) sixty-three letters to Mother Rosa Gattorno,

b) eleven letters to some Sisters,

c) four letters to others.

a) Letters to Mother Rosa Gattorno

The occasions for writing to the Foundress are the most varied, and all concern the facts and topics of everyday experience.

There are very brief letters, in which she gives simple notices, and other longer ones, full of personal confidences, of reflections on how the Communities are going and on the Sisters' apostolic work; letters in which the Servant of God timidly offers some suggestion, sometimes anticipating the Foundress's decisions; and others in which she answers questions or explicit requests; or in which she asks forgiveness for some shortcoming, or for timely decisions taken without first consulting her.

Even in their sparse wording, the letters do not lack a charismatic breath, joined to great attention and delicate understanding for the sufferings and trials experienced by the Foundress, for the vicissitudes of the Institute, of the Communities, of the Works, and of the individual Sisters she followed personally with maternal solicitude, with discretion, with respect for all.

Always concerned about the Sisters' health and their fidelity to their vocation, Sister A. del Salvatore accompanies them constantly with a mother's heart in the places where they work, taking on - to the very end - responsibility for their lives, their labors, and their difficulties, giving the Foundress prompt word of all this.

1) The Servant of God writes that she feels incapable of the office entrusted to her, but is ready to obey.

She writes that the Sisters are well and good, the girls are studying; she will have the doctor see some of them. She states that Sister Anna Angela takes great care of the school (Proc. p. 1070).

[Sampierdarena, 1872-73]

Dearest Mother,

I come with this, my first letter, to tell you that I found myself truly in a muddle, dear mother, for I kept saying to myself: poor thing, so incapable, how will I manage, though gladly I do the obedience. Dear Mother, I tell the Lord to do it for me, that all will go well, then I tell the Holy Mother to guide me, and that, for love of God, she make me do everything well.

I beg you, dear Mother, to forgive my scribbles, I don't know if you'll make sense of me. Be cheerful, dear mother, for Jesus will see to everything in these 20 days.... The sisters are all well, they're good, the little girls are studying, all are well except Patelani, who is almost always in bed, her hands and feet are swollen, I don't know what to do with her, I thought of telling the doctor.

Saturday the sisters doing the collection brought in four lire; I went to Mr. Balladie about the kitchen, but didn't find him home; I'll go again tomorrow... Then we have four sick ones, I try to send someone one night and skip the next. I'd have so many things to tell you, but I'm afraid of bothering you. Sister Anna Angela teaches school and takes great care of it.

Mother, I tell you, as for the fast, right now I'm being lazy about it... it's better to work as I used to, go out begging alms; but do with me as you see fit: ready and obedient to your word. Dear mother, next time I'll write better; nothing is left for me but to greet you, and then, for all the sisters, I ask your blessing. Goodbye.

The girls have school twice a day, in the morning from nine to half past ten, in the evening it lasts longer... Patelani, if you allow, I'll have her taken to be seen by the doctor, while I have Putapullia and Nolli and Devoti examined too, because it seems to me the same trouble, then I'll do as you tell me, for in everything I want to obey you. Mother, right now Sister Anna Ippolita is in charge of cleaning, but I... Dear Mother, I told the sisters I want the girls and the dormitories kept clean... that if in the evening they're tired, they should say so, and then I won't send them to the night watch. Mother, I may have gotten it wrong...

I'll close, because I always think of more to say, so goodbye, dear mother... and I implore your powerful blessing. I am your most obedient daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

2) The Servant of God says she has received your letter and, as you directed, is taking lessons from Sister Anna Angela. Sister Anna Ippolita is very ill and she must watch over her continually; the other sisters are well and very good. A niece of Don Accinelli is ill and she has had to send her to the hospital. As confessor they now have a Jesuit and are very pleased; Providence is not lacking (Proc. p. 1065).

[from Sampierdarena, 1873]

A. M. F.

L.B.D.N.P.E.S.I.D.N

Blessed be our Glorious Mother St. Anne

May she ever be blessed

Dearest Mother,

at last I received your dear letter, what luck... Yes, dear Mother, I understood your wish... that I learn, yes, I shall learn. Last night I began, Sister Anna Angela gives me lessons, I shall learn so as to be able to do the will of my superiors...

Mother, I'll leave out the account of the missionaries' confessor, because I heard you already know it; I too had written the letter, but with all my work I forgot to send it to you, because Sister Anna Ippolita went four days without speaking, I truly believed she was going to die on me; I couldn't leave her a single moment, neither night nor day. I sent for the parish, Don Luigi came... he too gave me a fright, he's sleeping over there... in the morning he gave her the viaticum... and had the Holy Oil brought... then I sent for the doctor... he's already come three times, today, Saturday, he found her better...

The others are well, all good, truly all good... they're all under my charge, poor me... The girls really are studying, and the niece of don Accinelli, the doctor said her arm would have to be cut off... the first time I paid no attention, the second time he told me there was no more time to lose, so I took the girl, went straight to don Accinelli and gave him the doctor's report, he told me to take her to the hospital, I told him I'd take her to the doctor in Genoa every day... but he told me it's better she be in the hospital, that I should send her with some sister, I sent her at once with Sister Anna Angela, I was sad about it.

Dear Mother, don Accinelli told me about the confessor, he suggested Father Luigi, a Jesuit, and I told you, he told me to go, I went... today, Saturday, he came, he's all attentive and all eager for the institute and to have the rules observed; the Sisters are all pleased.

Mother, Providence comes modestly, in three days they brought me sixty francs; the other days they always bring me something. I went to the butcher, he told me 40 francs was too little, and I told him I'd give him 85, so long as he wrote off 100; then he said no, and I told him I'd give him 40 a month, then he said yes, he wrote off 100 francs and then had the meat given for the girls... it seemed to me there was some arrangement between them.... he left me a 15 percent cut, you'll scold me for it, mother...

Mr. Baladie has sent the kitchen utensils and everything's finished now.... the kitchen, Mother, tell me: should I send the girls to visit the sepulchers?.... Mother, the relatives of the girl from Sestri asked me if I'll let her go home for two or three days, if it seems right I'll say no, or else I'll send them to don Accinelli...

Mother, they suggested I go pay a visit to the mayor and the secretary, because the hospital is finished, should I go or not... Mother... I'll do as you say. In the dormitories, every day I have the cleaning done; every two weeks I have all the pillows washed, the classrooms, the refectory, the sheets, then all the beds... then, dear Mother, I'll do everything just as my dear Mother tells me, there's nothing more for me to say to you...

By the way, I was forgetting: St. Anne's little purse is growing, every day I put in 1 franc... and then our great treasure stands at Li. 100... Mother, the sisters all send their greetings, especially sisters Concetta and Giuseppa, and then all the others... My Mother, how is Sister Anna Vincenza, dear little Carlottina is well, and the superior Eletta di Gesù... I hope they're all well. Mother, please accept my most heartfelt greetings, dear mother, and from all the sisters... Goodbye, these 40 days have already gone by... forgive me, mother, goodbye... I am your Daughter forever. Goodbye...

Sister Anna del Salvatore

3) The Servant of God thanks Mother Gattorno for having sent her to Sestri, where she is doing very well; her health has improved. She confides to her the temptation she had to return to her family: now, however, it has all passed, and she thanks her for her charity (Proc. p. 1069).

[Sestri Ponente, 1873]

A. M. F.

Dearest Mother

Just two lines so as not to tire you, only to tell you that we arrived at Sestri at night. Mother, I thank you that, through no merit of mine, you sent me to Sestri, where I'm very glad to be... and I really feel the air does my health so much good. Mother, I found a superior all full of charity. Mother, I have nothing to say about the schedule, I mean to say be at ease, except in the morning, because truly it can't be done, but once we're in the other house you'll see things will go better, because we'll be near the church, so the schedule will be kept more exactly... Mother, forgive me if I've said something unbecoming of me.

Mother, as for my legs, I'm better, I move my ankle more easily. Mother, forgive me for what I told you, that is, that I had that ugly temptation to go home. I confess, dear mother, my sin, that for a long time now I had had this temptation, especially when I saw the superior give me a sour look... Mother, I'll stop, because I can't go on any more, from sobbing... But now it has all passed, and for it I thank God first and then you, dear mother, who with such charity knew how to take from me that temptation the like of which I had never felt in five years... Dear Mother, I shall never have tongue enough to thank you for so much charity shown to me...

My dear mother, I beg you to forgive these scribbles of mine, and forgive me if I've troubled you with this letter of mine. I'll close by wishing you a good rest of the year and a most happy journey... and I ask your blessing for me and for all the sisters. I'd have other things to tell you, but I fear becoming too tiresome.

I count myself your most ungrateful and thankless daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

4) The Servant of God has delayed writing to the Foundress so as to give her good news. She reports that they have not yet received calls to attend the sick at home.

She paid a visit to Mons. Giovannini, who encouraged her, promising her his full support.

The Servant of God then praises the goodness of the sisters (Proc. p. 722).

[Florence] 5 November [sic: recte December 1875]

A. M. F.

Dearest Mother,

Here I am again before you, my so dear Mother, with four scribbles of mine, to give you news of the house...

To my very great sorrow, I must tell you we still have no sick to attend. Believe me, good mother, I feel great sorrow over it... In fact, yesterday, Saturday, I went to see Mons. Giovannini, and indeed he received us with such familiarity, gave us his blessing and then told us to be at ease, that soon enough too many will come and we won't know what to do, then he told me he'd mention it to the parish priests, but that for the most part it's outsiders who'll ask, since city folk aren't in the habit of it, and indeed he told me there are many such cases but they're little sought after. Then he told me he'd already heard of us from the Marchesa Torregiani and the Marchesa Covoni Carolina, then he told us that, should he fall ill, he wants the Daughters of St. Anne, then he told us not to fail to go see him, that for the Daughters of St. Anne there will always be:

I don't know if you can make out these chicken scratches of mine. Mother, I delayed writing because I thought I could give you good news, but what can I do, I see that so far I can't; oh well, let's hope all will go well... For now there's nothing more for me to tell you. For Mass we go to San Barnaba, at half past seven, which is the nearest church.

The Sisters are well and good... I'll close by asking your pardon for my blunders. Be so kind as to receive my most sincere greetings, imploring your maternal blessing, I consider myself

Your most affectionate Daughter

Sister Anna Salvatore Orsi

5) The Servant of God informs the Mother that they are caring for a canon recommended by the Archbishop, for whom they must provide everything since he has no relatives (Proc. p. 1075).

[Florence, December 1875]

A. M. F.

Dearest Mother

Just two lines so as not to tire you, and to give you good news, which I believe will please you... Today, Friday, a new patient arrived... recommended by Mons. Archbishop. And he is a canon, one can hardly say all the recommendations the Archbishop has made. Indeed, he sent a carriage to fetch us with another priest. And then he himself came in person to visit this sick man. He wants attendance night and day. He is alone and has received the Holy Oil. The leading gentlemen of Florence come to visit him.

Mother, my own, here are the words Monsignor had me told, namely that what he wants done is this: to watch over his belongings and do everything as if it were our own. In fact he wanted to give me money, to buy things for the sick man. As well as to keep the accounts and do all that is needed. And I answered him that, as for the sick man, we can do everything, but keeping the money we cannot do. And he said he puts it into our hands.

Just imagine, dear Mother, I find myself almost in a tangle, because I can't leave him for a moment... because there is a woman and two daughters, whom I've noticed making things disappear, so advise me how I should act, because those two Sisters I can't trust: yes, they're good, but for the sick man they have no capacity, especially since the Archbishop told me they're good with the sick and I told him yes, they are good, but don't be alarmed, Mother, I hope all will go well.

Yesterday the Covoni lady came, but didn't find me in, perhaps she'll come again today. If she comes, I'll be able to tell you what she says to me, or whether she's really brought me something. For now there's nothing more for me to say... I don't know if you've really understood me. I ask you to accept a thousand greetings together with the good Sisters, and a thousand embraces. Imploring your maternal blessing, I consider myself

Your most affectionate Daughter

Sister Anna Salvatore Orsi

6) The Servant of God fears she is not living up to the Mother's trust. She reports having been with the Archbishop, who took great interest in the community; as well as with some ladies who bring offerings and collect them among friends.

She also points out that, because of the care of the sick, they are not always able to keep to the set schedule (Proc. p. 724).

[Florence] 24 December 1875

A. M. F.

Dearest Mother,

Ever since I heard your so dear letter addressed to me, I've found no peace, because I'm always afraid of not pleasing you, since you told me in the letter that you were always in distress. How this grieves me, Mother.

Today I went to pay my holiday greetings to Mons. Archbishop. Will I have done wrong? He asked me many things about the sick man, and I told him everything I was asked, and he told me to try to please him as much as I can, because he's such a good man and deserves every attention, and then he told me he was very pleased. Then he told me he cares about the house and that it would be better to wait for him himself to tell me when I should set it free. He gave us his blessing and then told us to come to him for anything at all, to always go to him.

Then I went to the Marchesa Rispoli, she gave me five lire, and then to Signora Severini, she gave me 5 lire and 2 flasks of wine; then she told me that today she'd go see certain ladies who would give her something; indeed, Mother, the day before yesterday she brought along a countess, and this one is simply mad about us; the Marchesa Covoni came herself and brought me a cake, which I'll send on to you, dear Mother... and I beg you to accept it, and along with it we send our Christmas holiday greetings. Forgive me, dear mother, the liberty I'm taking, but what can I do, I'm glad for you to enjoy this little thing, for the first time.

Most kind Mother, I ask you a great favor, though only if you think it right, and it is this: that Signora Severini earnestly begs that you send her the Holy Father's blessing, for her and her whole family. Forgive me, mother, if I was wrong to mention this to you, but what can I do, she begged so much I couldn't say no. You then do as you think best. As for me, Monsignor told me that the Covoni lady has found something for us.

There's nothing left for me but to wish you a happy Christmas, you and dear little Carlottina and Sister Anna Benedetta. Imploring your blessing for all

Your affectionate Sister Anna Salvatore Orsi

Postscript

I'll give you a report on the sick man. He's better, tomorrow he's getting up again; often the schedule can't be kept because he gets up at half past eleven, for us that's too awkward an hour, and so we have to wait until he's in bed.

Goodbye, Mother. I send you my greetings, to you, to Carlottina and to Sister Anna Benedetta. A letter from you to set my mind at ease would be most welcome.

7) The Servant of God tells the Mother she cannot write very often because of the work, of which she gives a detailed account. She reports that a countess would like the Daughters of St. Anne for the religious instruction of boys, and that Princess Strozzi brought an alms-gift and set before them the plan of entrusting the Sisters with a school for the blind (Proc. p. 726).

[Florence] 28 December 1875

A. M. F.

Dearest Mother,

For several days now I had been longing for a letter from you, because I feared you were displeased. But, thank God, I have just this moment received one, which brought me such joy. Believe me, dear Mother, it has taken a great weight off me.

I also gather you'd like my letters more often. But what can I do, believe me, I haven't a moment to spare, because that blessed canon cannot be left, because when the Daughters of St. Anne aren't there he says there's no one, and so we always go there; in the morning we leave the house at a quarter to seven, and sometimes even at seven or half past, we go to make our Holy Communion, and then, as soon as we've had breakfast, we go straight back to him, sometimes we stay until noon and other times we have to stay until one. The reason for this is that he gets up late. So before his bed is made and he's been given something to eat, the hour's soon upon us.

Dear Mother, yesterday the Countess came - I don't recall her name now - and she's absolutely mad about the Daughters of St. Anne, and told me she's spoken with many ladies of the congregation and they'd like a school to instruct them in religion. They'd give the premises free of charge, she says it's in the center of the city, then she told me two or three of those parish priests would themselves send their pupils; what can one say, mother, they say it would do a lot of good, and I told her I'll speak to the mother about it, and then we'll do whatever the mother says. Perhaps tomorrow morning she'll come again to find out something, but I told her that once you've written to me, I'll be able to tell her something.

Then, today itself, Princess Strozzi came, gave me 20 lire, and then told me she's thought of giving the direction of these blind people to nuns, and so she's thought of taking the Daughters of St. Anne because she believes them the most suited, and that for now she'd need three, and later she'd hope to grow this pious work. Then she left asking me to let her know something soon...

We have another sick woman. She's very ill... in fact, I don't know if she'll still be alive tomorrow.

I'll close this letter of mine asking your forgiveness for every fault of mine. I send you my most heartfelt greetings, together with the dear Sisters... Believe me

I am your unworthy Daughter

Salvatore Orsi

Postscript

Relatives of Sister Anna Nastasia came; they brought me a letter with a money order inside, sent by the parish priest of Peccioli, with Sister Anna Benedetta's address; I've sent it on to her together with the sweet bread.

8) She writes that she was received by the Archbishop with great kindness; he has promised his help in finding premises suited to the community, but finds it difficult for the boys to be taught at school past the age of seven. He will soon send her the permit to take up collections (Proc. p. 1071).

[Florence, 1875-1876]

A. M. F.

Most beloved Mother,

Here I am to give you news of everything Mons. Archbishop told me. He received me with such kindness... I told him everything just as I was told to say, and he told me he approves of it all, and then told me that for now it isn't so easy to find a little apartment suited to us, and so we must still have a little patience, but that meanwhile he will take every care to be able to find one.

Then he told us he's not pleased about schooling for children from seven to eleven years of age. It's difficult in this city... For girls, yes, but boys... past seven, no, or else it could be done as a kind of day-shelter. Then he told me how we're doing and that we shouldn't lose heart, that he hopes everything will go well... Then I told him, about the collection, the exact words I was told to say to him, and he told me that in a few days he'll send me the permit, and that he's had to write to Rome because elsewhere he couldn't get anything. But he has good hope. And as soon as it arrives he'll send it to me.

Then he asked me whether I had been to see the Baldovino lady and the Marchesa Toreggiani, and Princess Strozzi, and I told him that with the Strozzi lady yes, I'd gone, but not with the others, because the Covoni lady told me she'd take care of everything herself; he asked me whether Princess Strozzi had received us well or not, and I told him yes, and he was quite pleased. Then he asked me about the confessor, whether we're satisfied, and whether he hears our confession every eight days, and I told him yes. Then he asked me when he'd be coming there, and I said I don't know, and then he told me to give you many regards from him. And that you should take care of yourself, and he'll take every care for us. He gave the two of us his blessing, and then the whole house.

So, for now, there's nothing left for me but to greet you, together with the good Sisters, receive a thousand embraces in the Heart of Jesus

I consider myself your unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna Salvatore

Postscript

I don't know if I've made myself clear, Mother, but if not, I'll write to you at greater length another time. Receive many regards from Monsignor. And for Sister Benedetta.

9) The Servant of God is pleased that the Foundress accepts the Institute for the blind, and informs her that both the Archbishop and some noble benefactresses are making an effort to find larger lodgings suited to the community.

She suggests informing Mons. Cecconi of the new project for the blind. She closes by giving the Mother news of the sick and of the sisters (Proc. p. 727).

[Florence] 2 January 1876

A. M. F.

My dearest Mother,

I have received your dear letter. I gather you tell me you accept the orphanage for the blind. What good fortune, how glad I am. Believe me, because much good can be done with this Princess. For now, that is, for a fortnight, she's not at home because she had to go to the country, she told me afterward, and then told me that as soon as she's home she'll come see me, or else I'll go to her.

Yesterday, Saturday, the Countess Bergal sent me 20 flasks of red wine. Yesterday too the Marchesa Covoni Carolina came; she told me she's found some alms, but couldn't stay because it was late; she also told me that Mons. Archbishop is taking great pains for us, especially to find this house. Then she told me that today, at half past ten, she expects me at her house because she has many things to tell me, and afterward I'll write you everything she tells me. Should I say anything about this shelter? If he asks me something, yes, is that right? Especially since you speak with all these Ladies, because I wouldn't want the Archbishop to learn of it from others before learning it from us, isn't it true, Mother, that it would be good to let him know, especially since it really does seem he wants to act toward us as a father. Indeed the marchesa told me it almost seems he'd want to know even about the sick people we visit, because he really holds us as his own. But I won't tell him anything without your leave. My own Mother, am I saying something wrong?... Perhaps so, isn't that right?

The sick woman we had has died, and the canon is better, he gets up every day, but he still always wants the Daughters of St. Anne. Sister Anna Ermanna isn't very well, today I had her stay in bed, I gave her a purgative. The others are well. Today I'll also go thank the countess, will I be doing wrong?

There's nothing left for me but to greet you with a true and sincere heart, imploring your maternal blessing. I consider myself Your

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna Salvatore Orsi

Postscript

I beg you for a letter from you, because your letters are a great comfort to me. I don't know if you received the sweet bread with the money order, if not I'll be distressed. Next time I won't do it that way again.

10) She informs the Foundress that on 8 April they moved into the new house on Via Faenza.

She asks her to send some nurse-sisters to cope with the many requests for care (Proc. p. 743).

[Florence] 9 April 1876

A. M. F.

Dearest Mother

Two hurried lines to tell you that yesterday, the 8th, we moved into the new house on Via Faenza. We did the move in the morning, at 5 o'clock. Afterward we came back from the night watch; I gave the porter 6 francs.

Dear Mother, I beg you, if you can, to send one or two nurse-sisters, because we have two sick women to tend, one of whom is a baroness, strongly recommended by Mons. Giovannini, and the other a lady's maid recommended by the Duchess Antinori.

So I beg you, dear Mother, to send someone, because the four of us can't manage so much, and besides Sister Anna Addolorata can't keep up night watches one after another, and besides the house has to be left alone!... The Baroness is beginning to get up, but it's a long illness.

I'll close because I'm in a hurry, as I must go to the night watch and can't help it. I send you my most heartfelt greetings and a tender embrace

I consider myself Your Unworthy daughter

Sister Anna Salvatore Orsi

11) She apologizes for not yet having given news of her return journey. She thanks the Foundress for having allowed her to go to Piacenza to meet her, and for having sent her sister Sister Anna Fabiana to Florence.

She asks whether she might sometimes send to the night watch two boarding pupils who ask her for this with touching insistence (Proc. p. 772).

Florence, 26 November 1876

A. M. F.

My dear beloved Mother,

I ask your forgiveness for my carelessness in not giving you news of the journey right away, which went very well, I give thanks for it to Almighty God, but what can I do, Mother, I found a mountain of things to do and so couldn't find even a little bit of time to thank you for the great favor you, in your goodness, did me. Yes, my dear Mother, for as long as I live I shall keep in mind so fine a gift, your having given me leave to come there to Piacenza to see you, when I truly could bear it no longer without seeing you... And, what's more, for having given me my sister. My Mother, how much goodness you have toward me.

Dear Mother, we have 8 sick people, among them two gentlemen, from whom I hope we might get some help. Mother, yesterday the Marchesa Grifoni came to see us, the one whose daughter we attended, and it was a visit very pleasing to me because she brought me £100 for the care given to her daughter.

Then I'd like to ask whether you might give me leave to send the two Fossi girls to the night watch, because every day they come to beg me to send them. Their ages: one is 18 and the other 21. You can't believe the pleading they do with me, they even get down on their knees. And many times they say to me: so why don't we have the good fortune of becoming Daughters of St. Anne? Won't we too be allowed to give a little relief to poor humanity? Believe me, dear Mother, that many times I can't resist... So if you allow me, I'll send them from time to time.

The Sisters are well, as for me, I don't know how to put it, because seeing you brought me such consolation that you could never imagine...

I'll close my scribbles, always with the fear that you won't make sense of them. I send you my most sincere regards, together with the dear Sisters, and a thousand thanks from my sister, Sister Anna Fabiana. I beg you to give my regards to the very reverend Father.

Prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing and kiss your hand with reverence, while I have the good fortune to be entirely your

most wretched Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

I hope to see you soon.

12) She asks the Mother's forgiveness for having sent a telegram, moved by sisterly love, to her twenty-year-old brother, who was dying and wished to speak with her, so as then to die at peace. She now does not know whether he is still alive.

She reports that she has again sent Sister Anna Fabiana out collecting, and that the sick sisters are better and have resumed the night watches over the sick (Proc. p. 781).

Florence, 18 January 1877

A. M. F.

My dear beloved Mother,

Two hurried lines because it's late. Mother, I beg you, for charity's sake, forgive such boldness of mine, because at that moment I didn't know what I was doing. Ah, how I regret having sent that telegram! But what can I do, at that moment I let myself be carried away by sisterly love. But I assure you I won't let myself be carried away again; but what can I do, when I saw a dispatch arrive telling me my brother is at the point of death, that he wants to see me one last time to say a word to me, and that after having spoken with me and seen me he would die content and at peace... Then I learned from my sister that, before she too left home, when he was already ill, she saw him all pale and he asked her, and my sister asked him what he wanted, and he said to her: Ah, if only I could see Sister Anna del Salvatore! Poor thing, how good he was; he's 20 or 21 years old, perhaps he's already died. Tell me, dear Mother, what will become of that soul!

Mother, Sister Anna Speranza is in bed with her usual ailment, but I hope it will soon pass; I've sent Sister Anna Fabiana out again for oil, because there was still some village where half a barrel of oil could be had; Sister Anna Alessandrina and Sister Anna Filomena have not yet arrived. Of sick people we always have some. Sister A. Prassede goes to the night watch and is well, Sister A. Santo also does the nights and is better, the others are all well; of the House, so far nothing is known; this week we've always had Holy Mass, collecting alms about the City brings in very little, 2 or 3 francs. I'll tell you more by word of mouth, if I have the good fortune to come see you.

Prostrate at your feet, imploring your Maternal Blessing, please accept my most sincere regards, together with the Good Sisters, while I have the honor to sign myself

Your most wretched and ungrateful and unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

13) The Servant of God says she is ready to send Sister Anna Filomena to San Martinello, but notes that she is one of the community's best nurses and will need to be replaced. She writes that Sister Anna Assunta is very ill: if she is to go to Piacenza, it is best she undertake the journey at once, before it is too late.

Now even the well-off families of Florence are asking for the care of the Daughters of St. Anne (Proc. p. 784).

Florence, 9 February 1877

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

Two hurried lines to tell you I've received your letter, so welcome to me, in which you tell me to write to the superior of Perugia, that is, of San Martinello, to come as far as Ponte San Giovanni to collect Sister Anna Filomena. I'm quite ready, dear Mother, but how shall we manage here in Florence, where we have so many sick? Believe me, this good sister goes as far as four and five nights in a row, and does it so well that the sick are so pleased. Mother, I beg you to forgive me for telling you this, because if you take her from me it's certainly because Jesus wills it so. But, dear Mother, I hope you'll send another.

Mother, Sister Anna Assunta is getting worse every day and the doctor has said she is very ill, so if you mean to send her to Piacenza, unless you send her soon she won't be able to go at all; I'm showing you how things stand, but then you'll do as you think best...

As for that woman, if it doesn't please you I won't take her, because in Rome she knows no one; for sleeping, a sofa or a few chairs would do, since it would be for only a night or two at most; I was doing it because she paid my travel there and back.

Mother, we have so many sick; among them we have attended the lady Marchesa Giulia Serenetti [?] and Mr. Parenti.

It seems the gentry are now stirring and pleased. Countess Maria sends her greetings and perhaps on Monday she too will come; I delivered her letter.

I ask your forgiveness for every fault of mine; please accept, dear mother, my most sincere regards, together with the dear Sisters, prostrate I implore your blessing

While I [consider myself] Your

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

14) The Servant of God states that she has great trust in Providence: Jesus is her treasurer, he helps her and provides for her generously.

She points out that the requests for care are many: in three months they have attended to thirty sick people.

She closes by saying that the doctor wants to examine her because he suspects she may be ill with tuberculosis (Proc. p. 789).

Florence, 16 March 1877

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

Two hurried lines to tell you I think I understood I'm to send Sister A. Filomena and Sister Anna Teodosia to Montatedo; from what I gathered, I'm to dispatch them on the 20th and they must be at that station at 7 o'clock, where the Sisters from Genoa will also be found.

Dear Mother, it only troubles me that I don't know what province that is in.

Dear Mother, as for those 80 francs, I beg you not to worry, for I've deprived myself of nothing, though I hadn't expected to send any Sister; but be that as it may, I beg you to be at ease, that for sending the Sisters Jesus will provide, because He is my treasurer, so I think of nothing, because Jesus sees that I am an untamed little donkey, and so He thinks of everything Himself. Yesterday the bread bill came to me, and I burst out laughing, because I had only 30 francs and the bill was nearly 90 francs, but the Lord, so good, provided me that and even more... So I am happy, because I think of nothing.

Dear Mother, we have so many sick, and it seems to me the Florentines are vying with one another to have the Daughters of St. Anne at their bedside: from January until now there are already more than 30. The Sisters are well, all keep the night watch. For now there's nothing more for me to tell you; I ask your forgiveness for every fault of mine. Please accept my most sincere greetings, together with the dear Sisters. Prostrate, I kiss your hand with reverence, imploring your blessing on your whole community, while I remain entirely your

Most unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

Postscript

Miss Rovere sends you a thousand greetings, and will write that letter to the Cardinal, and perhaps she herself will come to bring you the 2000 francs; tomorrow the doctor, to my regret, wants to examine my chest, if you permit it, because he thinks I'm consumptive, but it isn't true, for I just laugh about it... May I send Sister Anna Anastasia on the egg collection, so she could get a bit of air?

15) The Servant of God writes that Miss Della Rovere still cannot send the promised sum; she is still lodged with the community because she is ill. She says she has had to borrow money from Father Bausa for daily expenses, and has paid various community bills in addition to the daily board.

She went to see the Archbishop, who received her well.

She asks permission to change the ordinary confessor, so as to leave Canon Niccolai free.

She also gives various pieces of information about some girls who will make their First Communion; the collection is going well (Proc. p. 790).

Florence, 29 March 1877

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

With great sorrow I must write to you that the 2000 francs have not yet been sent, because of the agent. You cannot imagine how much the poor woman suffers: she has got up from her bed to go find a new agent, so as to be able to send them as soon as possible, but she herself has had to get money from Father Bausa to use for daily expenses, so patience is needed; but be assured that it's certain, and she will send them; to me she gives 5 francs a day, then she paid the Sisters' fare to Civitavecchia, as well as all the telegrams, and some days she gives me 10 francs too, and she's still with us; she's quite unwell and always confined to bed. She tells me she no longer has the courage to write to you; I showed her your letter: she burst into unrestrained weeping, began to say: Dear Mother, I'd like to satisfy you tomorrow, for it weighs on her more than it does on herself.

As for Gigino, she has already spoken with Doctor Battaglia, and as soon as she can go out she'll speak with others. Father Bausa has come back from the Archbishop and again said to send her, and if she hasn't sent her yet, he'll go back there. But there's fear the Fossi man may have done some harm... But I went yesterday to wish her a happy Easter and she received me well, then the young lady will write me a letter of good wishes in my name and that of all the Sisters, so afterward I'll be able to tell you something, the same for the Marchesa Covoni.

Dear Mother, we have the special confessor, and he's so good, but he's a Missionary; the Sisters are all pleased. Until the octave is over the canon isn't coming, because he's giving the retreat. If you think it good to keep this one on, then I'll go to the Archbishop and have him let me keep this arrangement, and so Niccolai will be free. So I beg you, dear Mother, to tell me how I should act, because, once the octave is over, the Canon wrote to me that he's coming and wants to give the retreat to the First Communion girls, who number 4, who will make their First Communion; I've accepted one who pays 20 francs and another who will pay 22 francs; one is 7 years old and the other 12, whether I should accept them or not; the ones proposing them are two priests.

Then, as for the collection, I send Sister Anna Fabiana and Sister Anna Putamiena, because Sister Anna Speranza suffers greatly and has been in bed for several days now; the two of them do so much good, they bring me 5 or 6 francs every day, some days 7 francs. We have so many sick that one can hardly live: I've had to send Sister Anna Ubaldina three times, then we have several whom I never send.

Please accept my wishes for a Happy Easter with all the happiness you could desire, while I remain

your most wretched Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

Postscript

As for the half-price fares, I've already spoken about that, I hope we'll get them, and as soon as Miss Rovere is able to go out, she'll speak herself, and so it will be easier to obtain. I'm feeling better... Now peace has returned, the Sisters are fond of one another.

The Cardinal wrote me a lovely little letter.

16) The Servant of God takes the opportunity to send the Mother the postulants' money, from which she has deducted what was needed for the journey.

At Father Andreotti's request, she had the girls who had already made their First Communion on 3 May receive communion again, and for this she was sharply reproved by the confessor Niccolai, for not having asked his permission.

She reports that Niccolai will no longer come to hear confessions, and considers this a good thing, since he has always shown himself opposed to the Institute (Proc. p. 799).

Florence, 24 May 1877

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

I'm taking this good occasion to send you the money for the two postulants, who are good girls, and at the same time I ask you, if you can, to tell me when and with whom I should send them to Piacenza. The Capuchin Father's girl has only 90 francs, but he's promised he'll give something himself; for now he still hasn't given me anything, so I'm sending you only 250 francs, 10 for each I had to keep back for the journey, because for the moment I couldn't pay for their travel, so I'm sending 80 lire for one and 170 for the other, I kept 10 francs for each...

Dear Mother, a mistake happened to me, and it's this: the girls, having made their First Communion on 3 May, and believing that, once they had made it, it was enough forever; then, the next day, Father Andreotti, who is the one who always comes every morning to say Mass for us, told me, indeed begged me, to have them take communion again for a benefactor, and that he would do the preparation with a fervorino, and I, not thinking I was doing wrong, agreed to it; I did go, yes, in the morning, to see if I could find him to ask about this, but I didn't find him, and then Father Andreotti also told me that once they've made it the first time, it's enough, and they can make it a second and third time whenever they wish; indeed he begged me because he saw the girls so willing and well prepared... Ah, if only I had never done it, because Niccolai shouted at me terribly and then wrote to me that he wouldn't come anymore... because I do everything without his say, and also because I put the confessional in the church, so he could no longer secretly give out holy cards and notes. Don't worry, dear Mother, for who knows, it may well be better for us, because I know for certain he was entirely against us... I went straight to the Archbishop, but didn't find him because he is at Monte Senario, on holiday; tell me how I might proceed and whom I should ask for as Confessor...

Dear Mother, I have so many fine things to tell you, but I'll tell you when you come here to Florence; Sister Anna Speranza will tell you a little of how much good this Father Andreotti, one of the foremost of that order, does for us; I'd have so many, so many things to tell you, but time is lacking.

Please accept a million regards, together with the Sisters; prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing, while entirely your

it's true, your most unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

17) She asks the Foundress whether she may accept two girls.

She reports that the doctor has prescribed baths for Sister Anna Anastasia to keep her from taking to her bed; for now she still does the night watches and is good with the sick; the others are better.

She reports that in Florence a woman is passing herself off as a Daughter of St. Anne and collecting alms; for this she has been advised to file a report.

She asks permission to send someone to take up a collection in the Casentino (Proc. p. 803).

[Florence] 26 June 1877

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

I've wanted to write to you for several days now, but you well know how lazy I am. I wanted to let you know that the two Venturini girls, the Father has taken them home for this reason: that he can no longer pay. Yesterday two others came, one would pay 20 lire and is 12 and a half, and the other who would pay 15 is 8. Dear Mother, I beg you to tell me whether I should accept them or not; then I beg you, if you can, to tell me how I should proceed about Sister Anna Anastasia's baths. The doctor has prescribed sea baths for her, and if she's not sent he says there's a danger she'll end up bedridden; you then do as seems best inspired to you; for now she still does the night watches and does so much good for the sick. Sister Anna Bianca is better, but still has a bit of a cough; the others are well. We have so many sick.

As for the collection, it's always 3 or 4 francs, and some days 5, but now that all the gentry have gone to the country, very little is to be had; but yesterday I went to the Marchesa Stufa and she gave me 10 francs; the Marchesa Toriggiani sent me 22 francs.

I've learned that in Florence there's a woman who dresses like us and goes about the houses asking for alms, saying she's a Daughter of St. Anne, and Father Andreotti learned of it from other people, and tells me to file a report, because this woman is capable of doing harm and then having it all fall on us, and at the same time this official will give me the permit in writing, because he's such a friend of the Scolopi; the Father Provincial also says it's good to file a report, because this woman is capable of any kind of mischief...

Sister Anna Costanza tells me that, if she went toward the Casentino, she'd gather plenty of cheese, since she knows those parts well, she'd pass through her own home village and stay 7 or 8 days because there are many gentry families there; if you think it good, let me know, because now is truly the season, since there are wheat and cheese harvests...

For now it seems I have nothing more to tell you. I beg you to accept my most sincere regards, together with the good Sisters, imploring your maternal blessing, while I remain your

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

Postscript

I enclose the letter from those two postulants. I beg you, out of charity, to write a little note to the Chaplain, because only yesterday he bought a table for the girls' refectory.

18) The Servant of God is deeply grieved to be the cause of disorder in the community; she asks to be relieved of the office of superior, saying she is ready to do whatever the Mother decides. She acknowledges that she is never present at the common exercises, but does not excuse herself for it; she defends herself, however, against the most painful and false accusation, that of not being faithful to meditation.

She also informs the Mother that one sister feels tempted to return to her family; she gives the list of the community and the date each one took the habit (Proc. p. 806).

Florence, 9 July 1877

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

How great was the joy I felt on receiving your so longed-for letter, and just as painful it was to read it. O God, what sorrow, what great grief it was for me to learn that in that community there is so much disorder because of me. My God, what heartbreak... Ah, my dear Mother, if this happens through my fault, you, so good, could take me away so as not to give this scandal, and then this holy community will flourish and spread its most beautiful branches throughout that fine city; but I am ready to do, in all and for all, whatever you command me, and even should I have to stay for the whole of my life in this community, I would do so gladly, so long as my dear Mother is content...

It is true that I never go to the common exercises, such as the evening and midday prayers, but as for meditation this is not true, because it is I who do the waking, and at the Rosary, when I'm not at the night watch, I am always there like the others; but I may be mistaken, because if you say so it must mean it is true.

The Sister who tells me to send away - the one who comes from Parma - asks me to tell you that for a long time now she has wanted to confide in you a temptation, namely to go back home, but she never had the courage; however this morning she tells me she is calmer, that this time I should not send her away, because she has thanked me and then, weeping, begged me to say nothing to you, but it was my duty to let you know.

Dear Mother, Sister Anna Addolorata has left, but, poor thing, how she wept, because she said that word to Sister Anna Monaca in jest, and not meaning to be taken up on it... Dear Mother, I paid her fare as far as Rome, because I had no more, only a very few cents were left to me...

The list of the Sisters: Sister Anna Rosa Podestà was one of the first, so it will be 11 years; Sister Anna Addolorata, Gianna, I believe about 10; Sister Anna Stanislaa Vignoli, 4 years and 3 months; Sister Anna Elvira Persiani, 4 years; Sister Anna Costanza Cenni, 4 years and 3 months; Sister Anna Bianca Bronchi, 3 years and [some] months; Sister Anna Ubaldina Cavaciutti, 3 years and [some] months; Sister Anna Assunta Dell'Agnello, 2 years and 8 months; Sister Anna Ernesta Valeri, 2 years and [some] months; Sister Anna Valeria, [some] years... Sister Anna Narcisa Carnevale, 8 months; Sister Anna Casta Bertolotti, 8 months; Sister Anna Fabiana Orsi, 8 months; Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, about 9 years.

For now there's nothing left for me but to ask your forgiveness for so many faults of mine; I promise you fidelity... Prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing, while I remain your

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

19) The Servant of God sets out, with suffering and humility, the words she spoke which Canon Ciaranfi has distorted, attributing to her the decision to remove Father Andreotti.

She gives news of the collection and of the Sisters (Proc. p. 819).

Florence, 1 November 1877

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

A few lines in haste to tell you how I'm getting on here in Florence. Ah! My good and dear Mother, I almost feel my strength failing me, and it seems I can no longer hold out against this continual and fierce battle that my cruel enemy, the devil, stirs up against me every day... Dear Mother, how much suffering...

My dear Mother, this is what has happened to me: today Father Andreotti came to us and told me I had said to Canon Ciaranfi that there's no need for him to come give lessons any more, since the Sisters are instructed from Piacenza, and that if he wants to come say Mass he may, but otherwise not. Ah, dear little Mother, I confess the plain truth: it is not true that I said this. Ah, my dear Mother, I almost lose my faith, for I say to myself, what can I expect from laymen, when even priests treat me so? Ah, I would never have thought to find such insincerity.

Here I am ready to say what I said to Ciaranfi, which were these words. This man, so severe, began by saying he had learned that Father Andreotti comes too often, and that he's someone without experience who doesn't know the City, and that even Mons. Lamberti had met with slanders and had to stop going to see the Sisters anymore; and then he began to say to me: and for what reason? We want to run a School when we have no teachers, and why don't they have them trained at the Mother House? Then I, feeling that he was almost discrediting the Institute, grew heated and said: What? The Mother has no Teachers? Yes she does, indeed she has them all trained before sending them to the other houses. But since we learned that this Father is so good and gives his service free of charge, that's why we took advantage of it. But if I write to the Reverend Mother, surely she would send them to me at once, because the Mother House is well provided with teachers and nurse-sisters...

These are the words I said to this Canon... If I did wrong, then give me a penance, which I am most ready to accept, but without realizing it I may fall into this, because if the Mother or the Institute is touched I feel duty-bound to act so; and if this is not believed, I beg you, dear Mother, to ask the Sister who was with me, Sister Anna Rosa, who is not capable of saying one thing for another...

I'll close, for I fear troubling you or causing you too much sorrow. I beg you to accept my most sincere greetings, together with the good Sisters. Prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing

While your Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

P.S.

Yesterday, around the City, I found seven francs, and the sisters brought in three francs, and then I went again to see the Rovere lady, and she told me to tell you that she's keeping her promise about the 2000 francs, and that this week she'll give me something for myself, as well as pay the girl's monthly board... She asks me to give you her warm regards. The Sister left for Montone with the other three, as far as Ponte S. Giovanni. Sister Anna Giuseppa has arrived safely and the others are all well.

20) She thanks the Mother for the letter received. She would have told the truth even without receiving the formal order of obedience. The Servant of God is very grieved by the accusations made against her, but submits to every suffering. She has lied neither to Father Andreotti nor to the canon; she will go to the Curia to speak with Canon Ciaranfi.

She presents some postulants (Proc. p. 835).

Florence, 21 February 1878

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

Two hurried lines to thank you for your dear letter, in which you tell me to go to Canon Ciaranfi. Dear Mother, I assure you that, even without your having bound me by obedience, I would have told you the plain truth. O my Jesus, how glad I am that you let all the blame rain down on me and let yourself be left free and unburdened... O God, for my great sins everything is too little. It only grieves me, O my dear Mother, to be the ungrateful and cruel one who makes you waste away. O Mother, if I may still call you Mother, it seems that hell has been unleashed against me.

Dear Mother, here are the words Ciaranfi said to me: I tell you not to lie anymore... And why did I tell Father Andreotti it isn't true that I told Ciaranfi there's no need for him to teach anymore, and why do I never go to see him, when he told me many times to come on Wednesdays, which is indeed true, which he told me when I went to wish him the holiday greetings; I say it's true because I asked Sister Anna Giuseppina whether she remembered this, and she told me yes. And then he told me to go on Wednesday, because on Wednesday he's there at the Curia specifically to hear the nuns, and so on Wednesday I'll go, and then I'll tell you everything he's told me.

Dear Mother, I may have been wrong, but with you, my dear Mother, I have come with the plain truth... And besides, you are my Mother, and rather than betray you or be unfaithful to you I'd rather suffer a thousand martyrdoms... Oh yes, I assure you that even if you sent me away from your holy Institute I would love you just the same and be faithful to you; but rejoice, O Mother, for if Jesus allows these things it's because He wants you ever more holy, and to make me pay for so many sins that outnumber the stars of heaven! Oh dear Mother, I shall pray so hard to Jesus that you may come to know me through and through, even the most secret thoughts of my heart!...

Yesterday the inspector came, and the Covoni lady too, and she assured me things will go well, and that besides the outside schools the Municipality will also grant a subsidy for the boarding pupils.

Three postulants have come forward, but one has been in service for a while; still, she's a fine young woman, tall, strong and sturdy, and is 21, with a 500-franc dowry; and one is the niece of a Brother of St. John of God, but her dowry is only 300 francs, she is 20; the other is 27 and her dowry, I believe, is 500 francs. I also enclose here a letter from a young woman; you will do as you think best.

Please accept a thousand regards. I beg you to forgive me for so many sorrows I have caused you; pray that I may convert...

Your forever Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

The parish priest of Monticelli, the Curate, has had three most beautiful oil paintings framed for us: St. Joseph, the Sacred Heart of Jesus and of Mary; he had them brought from Turin.

21) The Servant of God has learned that Father Andreotti will no longer be allowed to visit the community, by an order come from Rome. She is very grieved by this; the community has begun a prayer to St. Anne that Father Andreotti might be able to return.

A new work is envisaged for the Daughters of St. Anne in Florence, and besides they have had other calls to attend the sick (Proc. p. 840).

Florence, 21 March 1878

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

Two hurried lines to give you sorrowful news that happened today, the 21st. My God, what grief!... Ah, dear Mother, what sorrow! Today the chaplain came and told me that Canon Ciaranfi had sent for him to see whether he would agree to come say Mass himself, because Father Andreotti is no longer to come. Oh dear Mother, what sorrow I felt and feel, I cannot explain it here! Ah, dear Mother, how many things one must still endure! What can this mean?

Yesterday, after lunch, he came along with another Scolopio, and they went to see the Church, but he said nothing to me, and today this sad news reaches me. The Chaplain says Ciaranfi told him he had an order from Rome to act this way. Tomorrow morning I'll go to Father Andreotti and find out how matters stand. Perhaps you already know. All of us have begun a prayer to the Holy Mother, that she grant the grace that his Superiors send him back again...

Today a gentleman also came to ask me whether the Mother will give him the nuns, because several gentlemen of Florence have joined together to open another House of the Daughters of St. Anne outside the Porta della Croce, though still within the city of Florence. Today the Countess Montauti came to call us, for her sick lady's maid and for a sister-in-law of hers, in her own house.

I'll close this letter of mine in the deepest grief over dear Father Andreotti. For charity's sake, dear Mother, tell me something... I beg you to forgive my great faults; prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing, while I beg you to accept the warmest thanks for all the kindness you always show us; Jesus will reward you with a most rich crown of glory in heaven... Please accept a thousand regards from your forever

Most unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

22) The Servant of God reports that the doctor has written her a letter of reproach for having let a sick sister leave; she feels caught between conflicting demands and suffers greatly.

She is very grieved that the Mother is ill (Proc. p. 847).

Florence, 10 April 1878

A. M. F.

Mother, my most dear Mother,

My sorrow is as great as can be said. Tell me, my little mother, how I should behave with these Florentines. Ah! Dear Mother, I no longer know how to conduct myself with these people!...

Here is yet another sorrow, and it is this: the doctor sent me such a sharp letter that it almost makes me lose my mind. Oh, believe me, dear [Mother], that for your sake I am ready to stay right here where I am for my whole life. Yes, my dear Mother, that because of these people I'd leave at once for Rome. The doctor tells me he no longer wants to come, because without his order I let Sister Anna Giuseppina leave with bronchitis, fever, and a chest complaint, and that she was a patient who could not be moved at all, and that I am responsible for this Sister's health; and I won't tell you everything, for it would cause you too much pain...

Dear Mother, I've just now received a letter from Sister Anna Benedetta; I thank her infinitely for the care and charity she always shows me, though I am unworthy to receive such kindness from my dear Mother... I'm sorry, and most grieved, to hear you're feeling unwell. O God, how it pains me!... I seem to see you lying on your bed with your terrible headache!... Ah, dear Mother, if only I could come see you, even for a single hour, it seems to me I'd be more at ease; poor Mother, how you suffer!... Yes, dear little Mother, I tell Jesus to make me suffer instead, as much as he likes, but to give you a little respite!... But, my God, what am I saying! Jesus wants you ever more holy, and so he lets you suffer...

I enclose a letter from that schoolteacher and a copy of her diploma. I hope that this other one we have here will also enter, at least so she tells me, that she wants to become a Daughter of St. Anne, and the wish has now come to her.

The schools are going well now, the girls, for the past few days, have been coming in great numbers... Of sick people too we have many. The Sisters are all well, all grieved that you're unwell, we've begun a novena to the Holy Mother for your health, and we shall always pray that Jesus grant you all the graces you desire...

I'll close, for I fear troubling you; for charity's sake, take care of yourself for the good of the dear Institute. Please accept the most sincere regards of all. Prostrate, I ask your Maternal Blessing, while I remain entirely your

Daughter, it's true

your most affectionate

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

23) She writes that she finds herself in Osimo, unable to continue her journey; for this reason she has asked the Bishop for lodging, and plans to leave the following morning.

She earnestly asks forgiveness for the sorrows caused (Proc. p. 848).

Osimo, 23 April 1878

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

Two hurried lines. Much to my regret, I'm here in Osimo and must sleep here, the reason being there are no horses, and I did not trust the coachman; but I also asked the Bishop's brother, and he too told me that for a day now everyone's away; I didn't know how to act, because if I went to the inn I feared the Bishop might come to learn we'd slept somewhere else without coming to his house; for charity's sake, good Mother, tell me if even so I was at fault, but finding myself in this situation I didn't know what to do, and I thought hard about the words you told me before I left, when I asked whether I should go see the Bishop or not, and you told me: if you can, go straight on and don't go there; but you did not, it seems to me, give me an absolute prohibition, and so I, finding myself in this situation, chose to sleep here, because had it been daytime we would rather have walked, but it was already 6 o'clock, and so I feared doing worse; so tomorrow morning we'll leave early, right after the Bishop's Mass.

With my heart on my lips and prostrate at your feet, I ask your forgiveness for such infamy of mine... O my God, I would never have believed I could become such a horrible monster, to betray my dear Mother so!... Ah, dear Mother, I assure you I shall weep as long as I live...

I dare not send you my greetings, but I only beg you, if you see fit, for your Maternal Blessing, while I remain

your most unworthy and wretched Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

24) The Servant of God was very glad to go make the spiritual exercises and never thought of avoiding it; she therefore does not understand why the Mother had to give her the order by way of obedience: she feels deeply grieved. She thinks, perhaps, that she erred in turning to the parish priest, but she believed she was doing well by asking him who the nearest Superior was. She protests her unconditional obedience (Proc. p. 854).

[Appianano, early August 1878]

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

Ah! What grief has just come to me, and quite unexpectedly. And how could it ever be that I would not want to obey, when I am so glad to be able to see you? And how could I go on living if, even for a single moment, such a thought had come to my mind? My God! After so much pleasure I felt on receiving the news that I was to come make the holy Exercises, I must now feel this sharp grief at seeing my dear Mother obliged to command me by obedience.

If I was wrong to ask the Provost which was the nearest Superior, I did not think I was doing wrong; quite the contrary, I thought I was doing well to ask this... I no longer know how to behave, I only ask your forgiveness, and only you can do with me as you wish; I am always and shall always be yours, and I am glad to do your will and not my own; if I must even come sooner, I shall be the gladder for it.

For now I'll say no more, because soon I shall be in your arms, and then you can do with me as you wish. Prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing. Please accept my most sincere greetings, while your forever

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

25) She has received the letter and the circular. They try to keep to the schedule; for health reasons she allows Sister Anna Protasina to rise later and go to bed early: she asks the Mother to tell her if she is wrong to do so.

She informs her that the Congregation of Charity has promised to give the money for the oil, while regarding the wheat she still knows nothing (Proc. p. 864).

Sermoneta, 16 March 1879

A. M. F.

Most reverend Mother,

I have received your so longed-for letter, as well as the Circular Letter, which says so many fine things about our holy Institute.

Reverend Mother, as for keeping the rule, we try to do all we can, especially regarding the schedule of prayers and the other common exercises; but as for the waking bell, I get up, but I let Sister Anna Protasina sleep until 7, and in the evening she often goes to bed before 8, and sometimes right after supper; I let her, because if I forced her to stay up I fear her fevers would come back; if, then, I am doing wrong to allow this, I beg you, out of charity, to write to me even just two lines, to tell me how I should manage...

Reverend Mother, as for the oil, yes, at least they have promised to give the money, but as for the wheat, so far nothing is known; we have asked them to give us the money, but still nothing has come of it. Tomorrow, after school, we'll go there and try to get them to give us the money, as you say.

For now I wouldn't know what else to tell you. Prostrate, I ask your forgiveness for every fault of mine, and I beg you to accept my most sincere regards, imploring your maternal blessing, while

I am your most unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

26) The Servant of God informs the Foundress of a serious situation: during the night watch over a sick woman, the sisters are molested by her husband. She asks to speak with her in person (Proc. p. 870).

Ovada [June 1879]

A. M. F.

Reverend Mother,

Two hurried lines to give you this important account.

As you will know, the sick woman has been taken to the countryside, and we go there to keep the night watch, but you should know it has turned out to be a trap set for the poor religious. This is already the second night we've gone, but besides the watch, so tiring in itself, we are molested by that madwoman's husband, who takes it upon himself to lay hands on us, and then says words I cannot explain here... Fortunately the Sister is faithful to the Institute; to tell you everything I can only do so in person... but I am ready to go there for as long as you wish.

I beg you, if you can, not to tell the Superior that I wrote to you. Please accept the most sincere regards of your

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

27) The Servant of God, with the sisters, arrived in Palermo after a painful journey; the welcome was exquisite; the house is very lovely and well furnished. She reports that Father Bova has already given them the monthly stipend; Father Zuccaro is not in the city.

She expresses feelings of trust in divine help and optimism about the future (Proc. p. 871).

Palermo, 4 May 1880

A.M.F.

Most Reverend Mother,

After a very painful journey, as you will already know from the telegram, we arrived in Palermo, where we were welcomed very warmly and with such courtesy I cannot express it; an excellent meal, as much as a weary stomach could wish for; the house is most charming; magnificent beds, refectory, kitchen, parlor, etc. — in a word, we lack nothing; Jesus and the Holy Mother are with us, so be assured that, with your prayers, we shall do everything well.

This very day the most reverend Father Bova came and at once brought me the 250-lira monthly allowance, and having handed him the account you gave me, he told me that tomorrow or the day after he would settle it with me at once, and then I shall send it to you immediately, as well as what remains from the journey, which I shall send you at the end of the month together with the household savings.

Father Zuccaro is with Monsignor the Archbishop in the country, at Bagheria, and cannot come before Thursday evening. So rest assured, my good Mother, that we are in a true earthly paradise. Only one thing is lacking, and that is a clock — we have none at all, neither a pocket watch nor a room clock, so I don't know how to manage the schedule. What do you say, should I buy one? I await your answer.

I'll close, because my head can bear no more; but rest assured, it was just the rough sea. Give me your blessing and believe me, for all eternity,

Most obedient daughter

Sister Anna Salvatore Orsi

P.S.

Please accept warm greetings from all the sisters, as well as those of the Most Reverend Father Bova, who earnestly commends himself to your prayers.

Here is the address: Piazza San Marco No. 8 — Palermo

28) The Servant of God reports that they have had their first call to attend the sick and that the whole community visited the Archbishop, who had fatherly words of encouragement, signing the letters of introduction to the parish priests and promising a visit to the house.

Father Zuccaro sends many useful things for the house, as does Father Bova.

She suggests the Mother write to Father Cusmano, who is proving a true benefactor, together with his religious Family (Proc. p. 873).

Palermo, 12 May 1880

A. M. F.

Most reverend Mother,

After a great fright, I received your comforting letter, which calmed me at once. Then I hear that you were not content until we had begun our nursing service, and behold, today, the eighth day since our arrival, Princess Belmonte sent us a sick woman, her lady's maid, and she is very pleased...

On Friday we went to see Monsignor the Archbishop; Canon Zuccaro wanted us all to go together, and he said so many fine things to us, and that a very large house is coming. After a most beautiful address he told us he would come to visit us. He poured out upon us the choicest of blessings, calling us by the lovely name of his Daughters... On Sunday the Circular Letters were made, with His Excellency's seal, and he put his signature on them; they were distributed to the parish priests, so we hope that all will go well and that the Holy Mother will assist us.

As for the collection before Monsignor, I haven't yet spoken to him about it because he left at once for Monte Cascini and is away for 20 days, but as soon as he's back I'll go there and do everything you told me to do when you left... Then, one day next week, this young lady, who does so much for us, is going herself with all the orphan girls on an outing to the country, and she would like to take us too; without your permission, I decide nothing...

For now Father Zuccaro sends something every single day: a dresser, a clock, a table, a washtub for laundry; then today I went to collect 14 crates of fabric for curtains, by order of Father Bova. I'll close by begging you to forgive every fault of mine. While I beg you to accept the most sincere regards along with the sisters, prostrate I ask your maternal blessing, while I remain forever your

Most unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

Postscript

I beg you, if you can, to give some reply to Father Cusmano, because this Family does us a great deal of good. Please accept a thousand greetings from Father Zuccaro and Father Bova.

29) The Servant of God feels optimistic about the future prosperity of the house; she writes that, in the Archbishop's absence, they have not yet begun collecting the monthly dues.

She asks forgiveness for a fault: on the occasion of the clothing of the Bocconiste sisters, she accepted a small refreshment for the community outside the refectory (Proc. p. 874).

Palermo, 24 May 1880

A. M. F.

Most reverend Mother,

Two lines so as not to tire you. I hope you've received my letter, in which I told you we've already begun our nursing service, and it continues steadily; so far there is still only the one patient, however; she is so pleased that to everyone who comes to visit her she gives endless praise...

As for the collection, that is, the monthly dues, we haven't begun yet because Monsignor the Archbishop hasn't yet returned. So we must wait until the end of the month; as soon as he arrives I'll go there, and then we'll do as he says. Canon Zuccaro always comes and always sends us something: yesterday, for instance, he sent us medlars, which he had picked in Monsignor's garden. So far we still have no confessor; he hears our confessions himself, then, as soon as Monsignor arrives, he'll give us one... And now, even as I write, another sick woman has arrived, and so I hope this house will become a great house...

Reverend Mother, here I am prostrate at your maternal feet, with tears in my eyes, accusing myself of a grave fault committed yesterday. My God! What a wretch I am... Here it is: yesterday the six Bocconiste took the habit, the ones from that Father who came to Naples; since they welcomed us so warmly when we arrived, they prepared everything themselves, and afterward almost every day they bring us something, I went with the sisters to greet them, and as they were coming out from lunch they asked me to let them have coffee; I gave in, so I had coffee, I and the Sisters, then they brought us fruit, sweets and other little things; for this fault I committed I ask your maternal heart for forgiveness and a penance, resolved never again to commit such a fault... but always through divine help.

Good and dear Mother, you forgot the book for the Confessor; I don't know what to do about it, whether you think best to send it, or else...

I'll close these scribblings by begging you a thousand and a thousand times for forgiveness for every fault of mine... I beg you to accept my most sincere regards; prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing, together with the Sisters, while, for all ages, your

most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

30) The Archbishop, writes the Servant of God, paid a visit to the community: he was very pleased and gave several suggestions.

She reports that she expects visits from influential ladies; the sick they have attended were all poor, so she has received no alms at all.

She wants to know the list of the trousseau to request from postulants, and asks that they be allowed to stay some time in Palermo after being accepted (Proc. p. 877).

Palermo, 24 June 1880

A. M. F.

Most reverend Mother,

Just two lines, so as not to tire you, because I can imagine how weary you must be... Well then, yesterday Monsignor the Archbishop came with his dear Canon Zuccaro, as he calls him, and he really did give us quite a surprise; luckily we were all still at home, and we were ready, because I always feared he would do it this way... as, indeed, the Canon came during recreation time, but told us nothing, either that he would come or that he would not...

He went to see everything, then asked us whether we were content and whether we had patients; finally he gave us a nice little half-hour talk, and then I asked him whether it would be good to pay a visit to the Mayor, and he told me to do it at once, and so I did, and I was glad because the Mayor received us so warmly that I promised him there would always be a place for the Daughters of St. Anne... Monsignor was so pleased about this...

And besides, today at five in the afternoon the Mayor's wife will come with Mrs. Napoli, and so we'll begin making a few acquaintances... I also spoke to Monsignor about the collection, that is the monthly dues, but he told me to wait a little longer, that he'd speak with the Canon and see what would be best, and then it would be done.

For now I have nothing more to say; there are sick people, but so far they're all poor, so we haven't received any alms. The Sisters are all well.

I'll close, prostrating myself; I beg you to accept the most sincere regards along with the Sisters, imploring your maternal blessing, while I remain

your forever most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

I would ask you, reverend Mother, if you could give a summary of the postulants, and whether they may stay here at least a little while, because if I tell them they must leave, they hold back and then don't come at all... The Canon says it would be good if you could send some news of those in America, or those in Pisa... Cardinal Alimonda will soon come here, to Palermo, so Monsignor said.

31) On the occasion of the feast of St. Rosalia, the Servant of God agreed to let Canon Zuccaro and Father Bova bring sweets, which they ate together in the refectory. She asks the Mother whether she was wrong and how to act in similar circumstances (Proc. p. 881).

Palermo, 15 July 1880

A. M. F.

Most reverend Mother,

Two [lines] again to tell you what happened to me today.
