Here it is: the Reverend Canon Zuccaro came and told me that, since these were three days of great feast in honor of St. Rosalia, and in this city it is customary to have sorbets and other sweets out of devotion, if I would allow it he would pass them round to all of us, and that at the same time he himself would partake along with us... and I didn't know how to behave, and it slipped out of me to say yes, because if I told him I could not allow it I feared he would take it badly, and besides it grieved me to deprive the Sisters of so pleasant a recreation, because he does nothing but speak of the Institute and of God, and always tries to make it grow...

So not only did the Canon come, but Father Bova came too, and they brought sorbets and sweets in quantity... and they had to be brought into the refectory because, the room being so small, there was no other way. So I want to know, for another time, how I should behave, whether I did wrong or whether, another time, I should behave the same way... Because here we have no space, and there's no other way, because the parlor is the size of a good table and no more... and besides, however quietly one speaks, it is heard and noticed by the others... because the Sisters of Father Cosmano hear everything, so there's no other means. But still, I'd like to know, if something similar happened to me for St. Anne's sake, how I should behave.

On the day of the Holy Mother we shall have a sung Mass with a fervent exhortation and the triduum with preaching and benediction...

Prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing, and forgiveness, if I was wrong.

Please accept the most sincere regards of the Unworthy

Your Daughter

Sister Anna Salvatore Orsi

32) She thanks the Mother for the spiritual Exercises and tells her that the mayor of Canicattì will visit to learn more about the Institute. She asks whether she received the letter from Canon Zuccaro, who wants sisters for a new work, and gives an account of the visit the community paid to the Archbishop, always most fatherly to them (Proc. p. 887).

Palermo, 6 October 1880

Most reverend Mother,

It's been several days since I last wrote to you; I wanted to wait so as to send you this small sum, 200 lire, and at the same time I take the chance to thank you for allowing us to make the holy Exercises. Only Jesus will reward you for all you do for the good of our souls. Ah!... yes, dear Mother, we shall try to respond, by making you happy, through observance of the holy Rules and by raising prayers to God for you, that the Lord may console you and grant you all the graces your maternal, generous and charitable heart could desire...

Dear Mother, if you can, I would like to know whether I should send the postulant or wait a little longer. There would be another one or two here, but they have no dowry, because the great extravagance of the parents leaves the poor daughters without one. However, they have a reasonable trousseau and are reasonably well educated...

Today the deputy mayor of Canicattì came and said that on Sunday the 10th the mayor himself will come to see how they are dressed. I hope you've received the letter from Canon Zuccaro, who wrote to you about having the Sisters at a most beautiful establishment; indeed Monsignor himself wants them, and he loves us, and calls us by the name of his daughters, because even the last time I went to visit him, as he was setting off on his rounds of visits, I brought all the Sisters, and he enjoyed this visit so much that he had us all sit close to him, and then he kept saying: tell me, my daughters, when will the Mother come here? How are you? Tell me, my dear little daughters, are you suffering? Pray, won't you, that your holy Institute may spread throughout the whole world... And then so many, many things that it would take a thick volume to tell even part of what he said to us, and then he asked me: when I come visiting, will I come back; and I told him that not only would I go but I would also bring the Sisters, and he liked this very much, for he said: Well done, my daughters, I'll expect you too when I come back on my rounds — will you come then?...

I'll close by begging your forgiveness for my great faults. I beg you to accept the most sincere regards, while, prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing, and kiss your hand reverently, together with the good Sisters, who are all well... and please accept a thousand greetings. Your forever most

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

33) The Servant of God says she is very grieved at Sister Anna Primitiva's departure: she believed it was an order from the Mother, not some superior's own whim; she therefore asks that she be made to return to Palermo along with other nurse-sisters. She further asks that a second teacher be sent for the new house about to open.

The community will immediately begin a novena to St. Anne for the Foundress's health (Proc. p. 894).

Palermo, 25 November 1880

A. M. F.

Reverend Mother,

I've just now received your dear letter, from which I see clearly that I have many sins to pay for... because Sister Anna Primitiva's departure weighed heavily on me... and I almost didn't want to send her off without a letter from you, but I feared it might cause you some distress not to send her at once, and besides, since it came by telegram, I feared there was a great need for her... and then I couldn't imagine that the Superiors might take such liberties. Ah! Dear Mother, I am truly most grieved over this... Dear Mother, I fear I misread the telegram; I'm sending it to you, and I beg you to read it again, for it seems to me it comes from Naples, and there's also Sister Anna Speranza, so, not knowing where to send her, I sent her to Naples...

As for the house, then, don't worry, because, being a house of nurses and there being no real need to write about it, no harm can come of it, at least I believe so, and I want to hope that good Jesus will help us and make everything go well. But, dear Mother, so as to be more at ease, if you should fear the house might suffer, while sending the others, since here at least two or three more would still be needed... so you could send her again... I don't know if I've explained myself... But still, you, dear Mother, do as you think best, because here it isn't like other places, where every time there's a change of some sister, this one objects and that one doesn't want it... but, on the contrary, here it's different, because they're fond of the Institute, and not of the Sisters, so that here it can change every moment and it will always be the same thing.

I'll take this occasion to ask you, if it were possible, to also find the second teacher for the opening of the establishment, at least that is what Monsignor the Archbishop would wish, at least for some time.

I beg you to forgive me for always troubling you, but what else can I do? I must tell you everything I feel, mustn't I?...

I'll close by begging you, for charity's sake, to take care of yourself, and for all that love you bear for Jesus... Ah! Good God, watch over her yourself... Ah!.. Mother, for charity's sake, your cough makes us all tremble... and we have no more peace... We've begun at once, with all our strength, a novena to the Holy Mother, and we hope she will console us by making you well again...

Please accept my most heartfelt regards, while I implore your maternal blessing; prostrate, I kiss your hand, while I remain

your most unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

Forgive the faults.

34) In accordance with the permission granted her, the Servant of God will act as godmother at a baptism together with Father Cusmano; all the sisters will be present at the ceremony.

She sends the Mother the accounts and a sum of money, and reports that the young woman who wants to become a Daughter of St. Anne, against her relatives' wishes, again asks to be accepted (Proc. p. 898).

Palermo, 7 January 1881

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

I've wanted to write to you for some days now, but time simply didn't allow it... I thank you infinitely for the two Sisters you sent me. Sister Anna Crocifissa kept Sister Anna Ancilla because Sister Anna Placentina wouldn't have been up to it. Monsignor the Archbishop is very pleased and hopes all will go well...

I would like to tell you so many things, but the shortness of time doesn't allow it. I wired you about that permission to stand as godmother at that baby's baptism, because here they're so scrupulous, and I feared Monsignor wouldn't want it. And I hadn't even written to you, dear Mother, about it, because I believed it simply wouldn't be possible, and I said frankly that the Mother doesn't permit me. This gentleman asked, out of charity, for your address; then he came and showed me the telegram where you gave permission to do this in your name... I also went to Monsignor and told him about it, and he too is most pleased, and told me: Yes, go, my daughter, I give you my blessing along with the Mother... So that tonight, in the presence of both communities, since this gentleman wants all the religious present at this great solemn baptism. So, in your name, I shall stand as godmother together with the reverend Father Cosmano...

Now I'm sending you two hundred lire, 200... I'm also sending you the accounts; I don't know whether they'll be exact, but I've tried to do my best to make them correct.

Today that Priest came back about the young woman who really would like to become a Daughter of St. Anne; he begged me to write to you again, and says that neither her mother nor her betrothed will be able to do anything... he says she is utterly firm... the only thing needed would be to get them across the sea right on the first day, that is, the very same day; I shall do as you say...

I'll close, because the post is leaving and I must go to the Sisters. Prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing and beg your forgiveness for every fault of mine.

Please accept the most sincere regards from me and from all the Sisters, while I remain forever your most

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

35) She thanks the Foundress for sending a nurse.

She writes to her that the house they wanted to buy was run-down, so nothing was concluded; Canon Zuccaro will look for another convent for sale.

She tells her that Father Cusmano, who came to see her, would always like to have the Daughters of St. Anne in the house together with his own religious, because he says they have brought him the Lord's blessing (Proc. p. 905).

Palermo, 21 February 1881

A. M. F.

Dear beloved Mother,

A hurried couple of lines to thank you for the Sister whom, out of your kindness, you sent me... As for the gift, I brought it to them and they appreciated it immensely... As for the house to be bought for us, the one that was for sale, it was looked at and it wouldn't be at all suitable, because it's entirely run-down, and it would cost more to fix it up than to buy it; so it's better to wait a little longer and find something more central, for the convenience of the sick; so Canon Zuccaro told me he'll now look to see whether there's some other more suitable convent, and then they'll do everything, that is, they'll write, as you said, to whoever it belonged to, and the name and location... Indeed, I'll give you some good news, which is this: since Father Cosmano is leaving this building, we might be able to stay in it, and then buy it. For now we're waiting to see how this works out, so we can settle in better.

Today Father Cosmano also came to see me and told me he'd be content to be more cramped, provided he had, in the same place, the Daughters of St. Anne too, so he asked me not to leave him, and that if they give him a fine convent, half of it will always be at our disposal... Because he says the Daughters of St. Anne have brought him God's blessing, and indeed when he calls us, he calls us by the name: O blessing of God, O blessed daughters of Mother St. Anne, and then so many other names which I leave out here so as not to trouble you...

The Sisters had a reasonable journey, and everything arrived well; I'd like to know where I should send whatever little money I can gather, which I hope will be 200 lire... as soon as I have it, around the 5th or 6th of next month.

I'll close by begging you to accept the most sincere regards and the warmest thanks for all you do for us, your poor but fortunate daughters, while, prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing, kissing your hand respectfully, along with the Sisters, who all love you... while I remain your most

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

Postscript

I was slow to write to you so I could be sure about the house they want to buy; I see that it was absolutely not suitable. Please accept the warmest thanks from me and from all the Sisters for the beautiful and dear holy pictures you sent us...

36) She reports she has received the letters for the mayor and the benefactresses: they were very well received. She expresses gratitude at being called to Piacenza; and also asks how she should answer Father Cusmano, who wants the Daughters of St. Anne but wishes to know the terms (Proc. p. 913).

Palermo, 26 June 1881

A. M. F.

Most reverend and dearest Mother,

I received your so welcome letter with the greatest pleasure, along with all the others... The mayor's was presented, and he liked it enormously. Just as the Princess was so pleased, each more than the other... and they all told me they want to write to you; as soon as I have the letters I'll send them to you. And as soon as I have news from the mayor I'll write to you at once. But I hope all goes well; through Princess Fitalia, who is his niece, I hope to obtain everything.

Dear Mother, I thank you infinitely for the good news you give me: first for the good news of coming to Piacenza, and then that of the two Sisters you're sending me; yes indeed, nothing is needed but your generous and motherly heart, which always thinks of our good... Now I beg you to tell me how I should behave, that is, how I should answer Father Cosmano, because he asks me to write to you, dear Mother, to see whether he might have the Daughters of St. Anne to help him, and what the terms would be. I told him to write himself, but he begged me so much that I had to promise him I would write to you. Please let me know, out of your charity, how I should answer him, or whether you would rather write to him yourself.

I'll close by begging you to forgive every fault of mine, while, prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing. Please accept the most sincere regards from me and from all the dear Sisters, while we wish you all the good your generous, motherly heart can and will ever wish for, while I have the good fortune to be, even if the least among your Daughters,

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

37) The Servant of God allows the Sisters attending the baroness Strabba to accompany her on walks outside the city, and lets others be driven home in a carriage with the doctor. She asks the Mother whether she may go on acting this way (Proc. p. 922).

Palermo, 1 January 1882

A. M. F.

Most reverend Mother,

I'm writing to wish you a happy new year, and not only that, but to wish it full of all those graces your motherly heart could desire...

Dear Mother, let me tell you what I've done and what I'm still doing regarding two sick women we have...

As I told you, we're attending to baroness Strabba, and she's mad, not always, but on those days when she's well the sisters take her out for air, because the doctor has ordered it; so she asked whether the Sisters might accompany her, together with her maid, through the city, in a closed carriage, and outside the city, but half a mile away from the city they let her get out and take a walk, on foot... May they do this or not?...

They also go to princess Carini's, and she always wants those same two; she too lives outside the City, and these, sometimes, the doctor from the princess's household has driven home, but in a closed carriage... for charity's sake, tell me whether they should go on doing this, because many times, while they're taking the Sisters home, they take one or another person too, since it's the princess's own carriage...

I beg you, for charity's sake, if you can, to tell me whether I should go on this way or not, as well as, regarding the Baroness, whether I should continue this way, that is, whether I should keep sending the sisters to take her out, or not; we give her almost constant care, and she's so prompt every month that she's the greatest benefactress we have: she gives us 50 francs. It seems to me that if we don't take into account those who can help the house, of the others we have many, but they give the house very little, almost nothing; so if I shouldn't continue, or if I did wrong in doing this, tell me how I should behave, and I shall obey at once.

I'm sending you 150 francs... and I would also ask you to tell me, as for the accounts, whether I should send them to Piacenza, or to you, in Rome.

I'll close by begging you to forgive me if I have failed, while, prostrate at your feet, I implore your maternal blessing. Kissing your hand reverently, while I remain your most

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

I'd like to know whether, in the accounts, I should also include those small things, like pasta, a bottle of wine, a kilo of bread, etc.?

38) The Servant of God went to Father Briuccia, a very well-off priest, and asked him for premises for the community, for a few months. He, encouraged by Mons. Celesia, immediately put at their disposal not only the premises but also the servants, for an indefinite time.

She writes that princess Fitalia is also showing interest in a house: she asks the Mother which one she should accept.

She suggests she write a letter of thanks to the Archbishop, and asks that more nurse-sisters be sent, because there are so many sick (Proc. p. 927).

Palermo, 13 February 1882

A. M. F.

Most reverend Mother,

Here I am to give you reasonably good news of our house in Palermo.

First of all, let me tell you that the day before yesterday I went to see a great gentleman: I asked him to give us premises for 2 or three years, or at least until we had found another, larger place, and he said these exact words to me: Yes, gladly, but only until the end of August; but right now, before you leave, go see Monsignor the Archbishop, and then I'll go let him know. So I did: before leaving I went and told him everything. Monsignor, quite pleased, told me: Yes, yes, let him come see me and we'll settle everything; and indeed he went; and I also went to princess Fitalia, and she told me they're in negotiations to buy us premises called St. Joseph's, which belonged to the Benedictine monks, but this may take a little while before we have it free [available]; so what do you say? Should I accept Father Briuccia's offer while they're buying us that other one?

This morning, then, I went to thank him, and he welcomed me doubly warmly, and told me that Monsignor wants him to give us the premises not until August, but until the following August, and then... So this man, seeing that Monsignor is so well disposed and full of concern for us, gives it to us rent-free, and not only that, but told me that everyone, both the porter and the other servants, will be at our command, and that, from today, he's giving us the keys... What do you say? Should we go there or not?... If you think it good to write a letter of thanks to Monsignor the Archbishop for his concern for us, it seems to me he will appreciate it.

I'll close by begging your forgiveness for every fault of mine, while I beg you to accept my most sincere regards, while I implore your maternal blessing, together with the good Sisters, while

I am your most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

I'm sending you 180 francs. I beg you, if you can, to send two Sisters, because we simply can't manage anymore, there are so many sick.

39) The Servant of God reports that on the eve of the feast of Our Lady, Sister Anna Albina Garavaldi died, having received every religious consolation; she died a saint's death, and all the expenses of the funeral and burial were covered by Canon Zuccaro.

She asks the Mother whether she might have Sister Anna Paolina return to the community, as she had promised, and tells her that all the sisters are waiting for her (Proc. p. 954).

Palermo, 9 December 1882

A. M. F.

Reverend and dear Mother,

Here I am to give you some news; I don't know whether it will be good or bad, but I hope that you, dear Mother, will be glad of it.

On Thursday at ten at night, the eve of Our Lady, Sister Anna Albina Garavaldi died. As you know she was always ill, ever since that congestion of the lung, and she could not recover no matter how much care was given; I assure you, Mother, that she had very great care. What a beautiful death she had, oh! Mother, she was attended and received all the Indulgences, the Viaticum and Extreme Unction, the Commendation of the Soul — in short, everything one could wish for one's last moments of life... a saint's death, such as this dear and most beautiful soul of God had.

For all the burial expenses, Canon Zuccaro thought of everything and paid for it all; I assure you it came to no less than a thousand lire, just for the church expenses and the funeral procession, not counting what the grave itself will cost, because between him and the parish priest Pizzoli they bought a burial plot specifically for the Institute, so you can imagine what an expense... Dear Mother, I would ask you, if you can and think it right, to write him a brief letter of thanks, because he really deserves it, as he does so very much for the Institute...

Mother, how are you, for charity's sake take care of yourself, yes, because your health is precious; and besides, if you fell ill, what would we do, since we're waiting for you here, all the sisters want you. Yes, we really do want you here.

I beg a further kindness of you, and it is this: since you had told me that Sister Anna Paolina was there only temporarily... and that you would send her back to me again, what do you say, will you give her to me? Should I go fetch her? Because I really don't know whom to leave at home when I have to go out, since there's also Sister Anna Artaria, who's well now, but they don't want her as an outside nurse, because they say she's Sicilian.

I'll close; prostrate, I ask your forgiveness, while I beg you to accept the most sincere regards from me and from all the Sisters, while I implore your maternal blessing

Your Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

Come soon, we're all waiting for you...

40) The Servant of God has received the letter with news of the death of the Foundress's mother: she expresses her deep sharing in the grief that has struck her.

She has sent off the postulants and sisters, according to the instructions received. She will tell the Mother in person about Sister Anna Albina's death (Proc. p. 956).

Palermo, 28 [December] 1882

A. M. F.

Reverend and dear Mother,

I've just now received your most dear letter. My God, what sorrow I felt on hearing about your Mama!... But good Jesus has already brought her to sweet rest, and she already prays for us. Yes, dear Mother, all of us shall pray, we shall all receive Communion and hear Masses; but that beautiful soul has ended her great suffering, she truly made her purgatory in this life, because of that asthma that always tormented her...

Mother, take heart, for soon God will console you, giving you the certainty of the beautiful glory your dear mama already enjoys in Paradise... My God, I wish... Mother... yes, I wish I had seen her... Ah!... oh!... Mother, what sorrow I feel... my God, my heart is breaking.

As for Sister Anna Albina, I'll tell you everything when I see you, but as to praying for her, Mother, this was her very first thought, and she promised to pray for you, Mother, and for the Institute. Yes, rest assured she will keep her promise.

I'm sending you the postulants as you tell me in the telegram, and Sister Anna Onoria, Sister Anna Angela, and Sister Anna Palmeria; Sister Anna Onoria broke a foot, so the doctor says she must stay in bed for at least 20 days.

You will find here the certificates and the postulants' money, minus 32, which were needed for the journey: 28.50 for the sea passage and 2 for embarkation, and two I gave to Sister Anna Angela for the carriages and disembarking. Please accept my most sincere regards and a warm kiss, while, prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing. Your most

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

41) She offers the Foundress her best Easter wishes, also on behalf of the community, and assures her of everyone's prayers. She also tells her that she asks the sisters who keep the night watch to pray for the Mother from midnight to one, because it is the hour most pleasing to Jesus.

She then expresses feelings of affection for the Mother (Proc. p. 963).

Palermo, 19 March 1883

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Mother,

I wish you, in the name of the whole Community, a good and holy Easter, with every choicest happiness, prosperity, health, and all the graces your good heart could desire... Yes, dear Mother, the prayers, if good God accepts them all, are yours. Yes, Mother, just as I am, I am entirely yours... after God and Mary, only you, Mother, and nothing more...

And to the Sisters who keep the night watch I also say that at midnight, until one o'clock, they should at least remember dear Mother, because those are the loveliest hours, and Jesus most appreciates and accepts them... How are you? You suffer, yes, I know!... You suffer very much, if that is what good Jesus wills for the good of the souls entrusted to you.

Mother, I'll venture to wish a happy Easter to Mrs. Carlotta and to the dear little children, most beautiful and most dear, and to the most precious treasures of the most beautiful and dearest Maria... Oh!... Mother, how dear they are to you!...

I'll close these scribblings of mine by begging you to forgive every fault of mine, while, prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing, while I beg you to accept the most heartfelt regards of your most

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

I enclose the accounts.

42) The Servant of God reports to the Mother that Father Briuccia escorted her to see the house, that is, the upper floor he intends to place at their disposal: it is very large and very beautiful; moreover he sent them to spend a day at his country house, providing the food and sweets.

The said Father is very ill, and the Servant of God suggests to the Mother that it would be good to comfort him with a letter from her.

She asks her whether she may give lodging to a nun from Agrigento who has come to Palermo for medical treatment (Proc. p. 974).

Palermo, 16 May 1883

A. M. F.

Reverend and dear Mother,

How are you? How do you feel now? My God, what enormous grief to hear you are ill... I hope good Jesus will make you recover soon, or at least ease your great suffering!... But yes, may Jesus grant us such a grace... My God, how we long for your health...

Mother, now I'll give you some lovely news, and it's this: on Saturday Father Briuccia came, and we went to see the house; oh Mother, how beautiful it is. Oh!... how big it is... I can't describe it all here, but I assure you it's most beautiful; you can already imagine from the rent these people pay, which is three thousand lire, 3000 francs a year, how big and lovely it must be... Then on Monday he sent all of us to his country estate, and he also sent his maid to keep us entertained, and he also sent us ever so many sweets, wine in great abundance, and an enormous plate of macaroni, liqueur, strawberries and fruit in abundance... Then he sent us home all the leftovers too.

Yesterday I went to thank him, and he asked me whether we were pleased, and I told him we were most pleased, and that we had enjoyed ourselves very much; and he told me that whenever we wished to go we were free to do so; then now he's sent us a most beautiful picture of Our Lady of Perpetual Help. Now, dear Mother, I would ask you, if you'd be willing to write him a short letter of thanks, because a single word from you is enough to please anyone, especially someone who has been so gravely ill; and he kept saying to me: but does the Mother know I'm so ill? And I told him I'd write to you about it... but how could I, when you yourself were ill? So I flattered him along... So if you write to him you can also put in a word of condolence, but he's well now... he told me he received the most beautiful wreath, and that it was very dear to him... but he couldn't write to you because of his grave illness with arthritic pains.

I'll close, prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing; please accept the most heartfelt regards of your forever

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

Postscript

A cloistered nun from Girgenti has just come, who had to come to Palermo to treat her eyes... She would like to come stay with us for a month or two at most; she would pay whatever is expected; what do you say? Should I take her in? In haste. Please accept a million sincere regards

Your Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

I hope you're feeling better, aren't you?

43) The Servant of God says she is in Termini, but about to leave, because the house is now going well; though there is much work, the Sisters show good will.

She reports that the superior is better, and that she would have liked to send some money, but could not because she found debts to be paid (Proc. p. 979).

Termini Imerese, 20 June 1883

A. M. F.

Reverend Mother,

A few lines so as not to tire you; first of all, how are you? I hope you've received my letter and that you've written to Father Briuccia.

I'm now in Termini since Monday, but today I'm leaving, because here, by the grace of God, things are going fairly well; it's true there's a lot of work, but I found both Sister Anna Giuditta and Sister Anna Gregoria full of good will. Now two examiners came to test the girls: they assured me they're doing very well. Today the man also came to prepare, and so I hope everything will go well and these gentlemen too will be pleased...

The Superior is much better, and if she keeps on this way she'll be up within a few days; the doctor also found her free of fever... So, Mother, I beg you to be at ease, everything will go well; the Superior asks me to tell you that these past few days she meant to send you a little money, but, poor thing, she found a debt of no less than 77 francs, run up by the previous Superiors... But rest assured that everything is paid... and she'll soon send you something.

I'll close by begging you to forgive every fault of mine; I send you my most heartfelt regards, while, prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing. Your forever

Most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

44) The Servant of God says it was a great grace for her to have been able to go to Piacenza and see the Mother again; the return journey was very lovely; she thanks her and asks whether she should send the money at once or wait for the postulants' journey.

She gives an account of the feast of St. Anne, and adds too that the deceased Sister Anna Albina enjoys great glory in heaven, and has obtained from the Virgin that the sisters prosper, especially in Palermo (Proc. p. 983).

Palermo, 28 July 1883

A. M. F.

Most reverend and dear Mother,

First of all I beg your forgiveness for not having been able to write to you right away, but I assure you it was always my most ardent wish... But my affairs, that is, my duties, were such that I couldn't fulfill so strict an obligation sooner. Mother, my coming to Piacenza was for me the greatest grace that could befall me. Yes, dear Mother, I would like to tell you something, but I know how great your weariness and workload are, and I dare not write to you at greater length.

My return journey was most lovely, truly lovely, because the company I had this time I have almost never had before... Ah! Oh Mother, how fine... Enough, when I see you I'll tell you everything... Yesterday, Friday, I received the payment; the Sisters thank you infinitely, and I too send you my most heartfelt thanks for the payment you sent me with such kindness. Yes, may good God reward you and grant you all the graces your most motherly and generous heart could desire...

Now I beg you to tell me how I should send you the money, whether I should send it by registered letter, or wait until I send you the postulants, or whether I myself will accompany them? In short, I'll do as you say...

Here for now all is going well; may Providence always assist us; it was indeed a great grace that even on the day of the Holy Mother a reasonable provision came, 105 francs, and before that nearly two bolts of metapolo, that is, white muslin, then they sent us I don't know how many ice creams. Monsignor Zuccaro got us several Masses said. He also passed the ice cream round to all the Priests and the Sisters; there was also a most beautiful sermon...

I hope the lady Countess Carlotta is well and has already returned from the baths, and that the dear treasures, the Virgin's little children, are well...

I'll give you some good news, which is this: dear Sister Anna Albina has obtained from Mother Mary that the Daughters of St. Anne, especially in Palermo, shall prosper... Mother, great glory does this one enjoy in heaven...

I'll close, while, prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing... and forgiveness for every fault of mine... Please accept a million thanks from me and from all the good Sisters, for having granted us the holy vows... and then for all the great good you do us continually, accept the most sincere regards of your most

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

Postscript

As for the Ardizzoni matter, I did as we had agreed, I spoke with the Superior, so you may rest completely assured there is nothing to it; indeed, they must go on just the same... but rest easy; I kiss your hand respectfully and send you my most heartfelt regards.

45) She has received from the Mother the letter with news that a new superior will arrive for Castelvetrano; she says it is necessary that she also send the pharmacist.

She reports that Sister Anna Della Pazienza died a saint's death: before dying she renewed her baptismal promises and her vows with edifying fervor; she promised to pray for the Institute and for the Mother.

For the funeral Canon Zuccaro made all the arrangements. The sick are always many, but the nurse-sisters are scarce (Proc. p. 995).

Palermo, 28 October 1883

Reverend and dearest Mother,

I received your dearest letter last night, and I'm very pleased to hear you'll send the Superior to Castelvetrano, so she can again restore the good reputation the Institute used to have; I hope you'll also send the pharmacist, because they're waiting for her there, since they say it's in the contract, and they've already dismissed the pharmacist; then you'll do as you think best.

Now let's get to our own matters. My dearest Mother, I give you the good news that Sister Anna della Pazienza flew to Paradise on 25 October, at nine in the evening... My Mother, what a most beautiful death... She asked forgiveness of me and then of all the Sisters, and renewed her baptismal promises and her holy Vows with the greatest fervor, a truly consoling thing to see... then she said that when they dressed her, after death, she begged that they put on her the oldest things, so as to observe holy poverty... and then so many other lovely things. So that for us it was not a sorrow, no, but a joy, because now we have another protector who will pray for us, and she promised she would pray hard for the Institute and for you, Mother... her body became so beautiful that no one wanted to leave her side... Enough, so as not to tire you, because otherwise I'd never stop...

As for the expenses, Monsignor Zuccaro thought of everything and paid for everything. As for Sister Anna Nicetta, then, Sister Anna Vincenza tells me that before changing the Sister she wanted to write to you, dear Mother, so I had to wait... Otherwise all is well; we have many sick and few Sisters. I hope, by God's grace, to be able to speak with you in person: not now, but whenever God wills... I know you're always suffering, and suffering very much...

I'll close by begging you to accept my most heartfelt regards, while I beg you to forgive every fault of mine.

I hope the Most Holy Virgin grants you what you desire...

Your most unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

46) She assures the Foundress that her little niece Nonni will be well, because she is protected by the Virgin; she knows she has suffered greatly.

The Servant of God thanks her for the sisters she has sent to the community and for the good she does.

She has learned that on the first of January the Mother must go to Rome, and she is happy because she will see her soon.

She thanks her, finally, for worrying about her health, while wishing she could relieve her sufferings (Proc. p. 998).

Palermo, 5 December 1883

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Mother,

I hope you've received mine. Yes, Mother, the Most Holy Virgin loves you very much, so she will watch over you, and Noni will be well. My Mother, I imagine how much the lady Countess Carlotta must have suffered. I assure you it seemed to me I could see it. You yourself went through a great suffering, because good God let you feel two sorrows and more... for you felt both the mother's and the daughter's. Enough, it will all end, and dear Mother Mary will not give you this great sorrow again!...

Mother, I thank you infinitely for the Sisters you sent me... yes, thank you, my Mother, truly good and capable ones, yes Mother, I am truly glad... I assure you that sending these five Sisters has done this community a great deal of good. Yes, dear Mother, good God must reward you for all you do for all of us, because you do so very much for us. Ah!... may good God console you and grant you all the graces your generous and kind heart could desire...

Your sorrows are enormous, Mother! I cannot bear to think of your suffering. Dear Mother, I learn from your most dear letter that on 1 January you'll be in Rome, and that I'll have the great good fortune of seeing you. My God, what consolation I feel, I cannot explain it. I wish December had only six days, so I could see you sooner…

I assure you that for me not even the journey to Piacenza seems long, no, to go to you, Mother. I'm very glad that now we travel in so little time, what a great advantage for us.

My Mother, I thank you for your concern for my health. You shall be obeyed at once, and I'll speak to you in person later, but I'm well now, truly. It only grieves me for you, who suffer so greatly!... and without my being able to give you the slightest relief.

Ah!... if I could be granted to relieve your sorrows and sufferings, how happy I would be...

I'll close these scribblings of mine, while, prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing and forgiveness for every fault of mine. I beg you to accept the most heartfelt regards of your

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

47) She has received the Foundress's letter, and the Servant of God replies, reassuring her that her brother will not die; on the contrary, he will be cured, because Our Lady protects him (Proc. p. 1008).

Palermo, 21 February 1884

A. M. F.

Dear Mother, ever dearest,

I've just now received your distressing letter, where I hear what you tell me about your Brother. My God, what grief! but your grief, my Mother, pains me more. Yes, sadly it's all true, but I assure you, in the name of the Most Holy Virgin, that your Brother will not die, no, and rather I hope the Most Holy Virgin won't even let him fall ill, and if he falls ill he will recover quickly, yes, quickly... and one "no" from Mother Mary is worth more than a hundred devils, so take heart, all will go well.

I beg you not to grieve, because dear Mary is already pleading, and Jesus grants her everything... Yes, my Mother, take heart, no, no, he will not fall ill, no, and the devil will be driven off, and indeed he's trying to do other things, but he won't succeed because most beautiful Mary does not allow it, no... no. It is not I who write at this moment, but the Virgin, who is here and smiling… and says you may rest assured...

I'll close, because I can no longer bear the pain. And you, how are you? For charity's sake, take care of yourself, for your health is our salvation. I send you my most heartfelt regards, while kissing your kind hand, while I have the good fortune of being your most unworthy, yes, but still your

Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

48) She thanks the Mother for the holy cards and medals she sent her, and tells her she obeyed at once her order to rest at least four hours, though she feels it as a punishment (Proc. p. 1009).

Palermo, 28 February 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Mother,

A few lines so as not to tire you. I thank you infinitely for the most beautiful holy cards and medals you sent me. Yes, my dear Mother, may good God reward you and grant you all those choicest graces your most generous and kind heart could desire... Your great kindness and immense charity toward me, your most unworthy daughter, is too great... Yes, Mother, I see clearly you do this to draw me toward God.

I hear you telling me to rest at least four hours, yes, my Mother, I am most ready, and I did it at once... Ah! My Mother, what grief... yes, what sharp grief I feel; I see in this a severe punishment for my great sins, and perhaps, indeed without perhaps, for the little profit I drew from it... Ah! My Mother, what sharp grief I feel, and what great shame I feel during that little time I spend before it... Enough, I'll close because truly I have no more heart for it.

And you, Mother, how are you? I know your suffering is enormous; for charity's sake take care of yourself, for the good of all of us and of the whole Institute. Assured that your brother is well, and the dearest little children too, and the lady Countess with the lord Count are well, I'll close by asking you to accept my most heartfelt regards, while I implore your maternal Blessing and forgiveness for every fault of mine, your

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

49) She gives an affirmative answer to two of the Mother's questions, assuring her that what she must do is God's will; she also writes that the Administration agrees to let Sister Anna Basilia go to Pignatelli, but a letter from the Foundress is needed.

She is very grieved at having left without having been able to say goodbye to her, and expresses feelings of humility (Proc. p. 1012).

Palermo, 7 April 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Mother,

I hope you've received my letter and the two crates of mandarins, and as soon as I can I'll send you the 75 lire for the little Madonna statue. I received your dearest letter yesterday, I understood it all because we had already agreed, and I hope you received my telegram where I told you yes, and indeed it is the truest will of God and the great pleasure of the Most Holy Virgin that she go to P. F., because she will find there in part what she desires, but not forever. But let her go there, and in another letter I'll explain myself better, but yes, I don't know if I've explained myself and whether you've understood me, yes, about what you, Mother, know, yes...

As for Sister Anna Basilia, then, the Administration is content, but you, Mother, must write to her at once, so that as soon as they have a letter from you she can go right away, that very day, to Pignatelli, and for those few days they must remain at the branch house, Sister Anna Placentina will take Sister Anna Basilia's place; what do you say, Mother?

Now I'm sending you a lovely sample for making stockings; since I heard from Sister Anna Berta that she wanted to have several pairs made for the Sisters in America, I'll take the chance to send you the sample, and if they are to be made there will be a great saving of time and cotton, so Sister Anna Berta asks me to do. What a laugh…

Now let's get to our own affairs. How are you? My God! I cannot explain to you the grief I suffered leaving you without being able to say goodbye… Ah, for charity's sake, let it never happen again; it was an enormous punishment for me, and I know I deserved it for so many infidelities of mine, yes, and I deserve worse, far worse...

I'll close, begging you to accept the most heartfelt regards from me and from the whole Community, that is, from all the Sisters, while, prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing and forgiveness for every fault of mine.

your most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

50) She relates that she was at Linguaglossa, where she found peace, serenity and observance.

She knows for certain that the Foundress is suffering; and assures her of her prayer to the Virgin for Carlotta (Proc. p. 1085).

[Castiglione, May 1884]

A. M. F.

I passed through Linguaglossa, but what a difference... There I found quiet, peace, and all the Sisters content, cheerful, and observant of the Holy Rule; much work and the schools full of girls, and always ready for prayers, for the rising bell, the rosary, the rest period; in short, I can assure you it's a pleasure... I told them to try to take their exams soon, and so the two teachers will join those from Castiglione, and so the Superior has promised that by the beginning of July they too will take their exams. On Thursday I hope to be able to go to Adernò.

Now let's turn to you, my Mother, how are you? My God!… I know for absolute certain that you've had a bad headache, and still have it…

I know that the Virgin's dear ones, that is, the dear children, are well and will be well, because the Most Holy Virgin watches over them... and holds them very dear... I hope the lady Countess is well, and that good God will console her... She still hasn't granted me the grace I long for, but I don't lose heart, no, no, I'll become a nuisance, but I won't leave the Virgin in peace until she has granted me the grace.

I send you again my most sincere regards

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

51) The Servant of God is very grieved at the news of the serious illness of Sister Anna Francesca Savignone.

She expresses sorrow that that person has not answered the Mother's letters, but believes it is God's will that she go on writing and accepting this suffering, also because her letters are well weighed. She also recounts a dream that seems to foreshadow the reality of the Institute or of a house, and attributes the effectiveness of the intervention to the Foundress.

She also reports other news (Proc. p. 1021).

Palermo, 14 June 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Mother,

With the greatest pleasure I receive a letter from you, but, oh what great sorrow, on hearing that Sister Anna Francesca is about to fly to Heaven and leave us alone. Yes, Mother, I feel great sorrow, because from here we lose an angel of goodness, but at the same time she will be our Advocate in Paradise.

Mother, ever dearest, I gather from your letter you still haven't received my letters. I'm so sorry, perhaps they went astray, but no, I know it arrived, after you wrote to me, where I told you something about all the houses, that is Linguaglossa, Castiglione, and Adernò, and then I begged your forgiveness for that mistake I made in wanting to send the sick Sister away for a few days to get some air, but I didn't send her, and I won't send her again without your permission first. I also received a most beautiful little letter from the lady Countess Carlotta; now I shall make it my business to write her my two scribbles, but I hope good God will console her, because he loves her greatly... truly greatly... And likewise the dear children.

Dear Mother, with great sorrow I hear what you tell me about that person who has stopped answering your letters; what grief I feel; good God wants this most beautiful sacrifice from you. Yes, he wanted you on the cross, as he himself was, without comfort, and alone, all alone to suffer. I don't know if I made it clear that it wasn't meant to be forever, but I couldn't understand that it would be so soon... Enough, I'm sorry to have to tell you that you still must not stop writing to him, because your letters are well kept... and considered most carefully... So he still doesn't want you to give it up... the reason I still don't know, why Jesus wants this harsh suffering from you... and suffering without respite…

Mother, if I weren't afraid of troubling you I would like to tell you a dream I had in Adernò; allow me to tell you part of it, and here it is: I fell asleep, and found myself in a great field, where there was a most beautiful arbor, resting on four columns and heavy with grapes, part almost ripe, part halfway grown, and part still small. Then, at the loveliest moment, a crowd of unruly young men placed themselves there, but the worst of them were six, all hanging from the columns, so that the poor arbor was leaning right over and almost ready to fall; my God, what grief I felt, I truly cannot explain it here, because it was ours; meanwhile, with great confidence, I turned to you, Mother, and at once you sent a person I did not know, but as soon as she stood on the arbor she immediately made war on them, but accomplished nothing, until she cried out loudly: and I shall call the Mother, and these, on hearing this name, withdrew into another vineyard, and there these wicked young men multiplied, and hurled fire and wrought great havoc in the middle of that vineyard, but the arbor, little by little, righted itself again and returned to its first freshness... and even to that vineyard they could do almost nothing... Because that lady who took up its defense kept calling on you, and so they grew frightened and had to flee in despair... I woke up so frightened I can't explain it here, but I fell asleep again at once, and, sleeping, I was telling my dream to a venerable person I did not know; she understood my account only halfway, and told me: this dream of yours is not without meaning, and again I woke...

Here, in part, is my dream. My Mother, I don't know what it means, however much I try to put it out of my mind, but truly I cannot. Mother, for charity's sake, don't read it, for you have no time to lose, too precious is your time...

Now let's turn to you. How are you? You suffer, and very great is your suffering. My God! What grief I feel; enough, good God will see to giving you that strength which is granted to you alone.

Now let's turn to something else. On Tuesday I took Sister Anna Gregoria to see Monsignor the Archbishop, and he was pleased, and liked her very much, so don't worry about Pignatelli, which is going well now, and I hope those women will be removed as well. Today he had a long talk with the Cavaliere, so I truly hope he'll remove them, because Monsignor has shown himself very displeased with those women...

Yesterday I spoke with Maria Teresa, and she asked me to give you her warm regards, and that she will soon send you her photograph; it truly put me to shame, because she asked me to pray that she might obtain a grace; do you see how humble she is?

I'll close by asking you to accept the most heartfelt regards of your most

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

Please forgive the faults.

52) She expresses feelings of great humility and reports to the Mother that the doctor has recommended Sister Anna Gemma's native air: she asks how she should proceed, and whether she should keep her in Palermo (Proc. p. 1030).

Palermo, 13 August 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Mother,

I wrote to you yesterday, and again today. I must write to you, first of all, to know how you are, because I imagine, and I'm quite sure, that you're suffering... it's true that you told me in your letter that for two days you'd been up, that is, out of bed, and without suffering; that word almost grieved me, because if the sufferings stop for a day, I'm almost certain they then make you suffer more, and for months... because the cause of your great suffering is my faults, and others', and misdeeds, but mine above all, since with my wretched life I am, sadly, the cause for you of such suffering, and for the world of so many punishments and scourges.

Now let's turn to something else. I beg you, out of charity, to tell me how I should proceed regarding Sister Anna Gemma, whom I had the doctor visit, and he tells me to have her change air, and if possible even her native air, or at least as close to her native air as possible, because he says she might perhaps recover, since she's only felt unwell for a few days and has only been in bed about three days so far... If then you, dear Mother, wish me to keep her here, I'll gladly keep her.

For now there is nothing left for me but to beg your forgiveness for so much wickedness of mine. Prostrate at your feet, I implore your maternal blessing, while I beg you to accept the most heartfelt regards of your ever

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

53) The Servant of God writes to the Mother that she has done what she could, but there is no way to get through to Sicily: no exceptions are made even for distinguished people, and it is painful to see so many people suffering; she tells her to send the tickets for Gaeta, or else only as far as Naples.

Out of obedience, she answers the Mother that it is not God's will that she go to Sicily for now, because she would meet with difficulties and dangers (Proc. p. 1041).

Reggio Calabria, 22 November 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend dearest Mother,

A few lines in great haste. With the greatest sorrow I must write to you that it's really impossible to get through. I assure you I have tried, but in vain, because these Sicilians are too stubborn. Imagine what grief for everyone. Even a regiment of soldiers arrived bound for Sicily, but they too had to turn back; it's truly a torment to see so many people suffering, who cannot get through, and indeed there's a general and a chamber chief stuck here in Reggio, but not even they can get through; they truly make no exception at all; so, if you think it best, you can send the tickets from Reggio to Gaeta, or you'll judge better, if you prefer, since they can't be sent as far as Gaeta, send them as far as Naples, because there we'll see what can be done; the cost in third class is 5 francs a day per person... 10 and 15... 5, 10 and 15 francs.

Now let's turn to something else; I hear you ask me, by way of obedience, to tell you whether you should come to Sicily, or wait another year? Here I'll tell you the plain truth: set aside the thought of coming to Sicily this year, because you would meet with enormous difficulties and great dangers of catching a serious illness, and then and then... So, for charity's sake, don't come to Sicily until further notice, because good God wills it so... and it is his will, though, if I'm not mistaken.

I'll close by begging you to take care of yourself, for charity's sake. Please accept the most heartfelt regards of your forever

Most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

Forgive me, I'm in great haste...

54) She asks the Mother's forgiveness for not having been able to write to her. She answers her questions: she doesn't know how long that priest will be her confessor, nor why he won't be any longer; she knows only that what is happening is God's will; what the Mother has entrusted to him will serve a great good. She informs her that she may now go to Sicily, since all danger has been averted (Proc. p. 1045).

Palermo, 26 December 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Mother,

A few lines in haste. For charity's sake, I beg you to forgive me, that is, to be willing to forgive me: I know, alas, the enormous fault I've committed these past days, in not being able to write to you; my God, what sharp grief... Yes, dear Mother, the weeping and the tears I've shed over not being able to write to you, I cannot explain here. Enough, I hope the Most Holy Virgin grants me the grace to be able to write, now...

As for what you ask me, wanting to know when I will hand them over, I really don't know. I only know that it was a true, most true will of God, and that it doesn't matter whether I hand them over, and indeed you must not hand them over at all, for now, but you, I beg you, be at peace. As for telling you how long he'll be your confessor, I really don't know, nor why he won't be any longer, forever, but I only know that Jesus is very pleased that you treat him this way... and let him keep what he has with him, because it will serve a great good.

Now as for coming to Palermo, you may come, because it has all passed; it was only because the devil wanted to leave you as good as dead, out of the great rage he bears against you, Mother, but now you may come, because the Virgin will not let him do anything, not even in Messina. Mother, I cannot go on with the letter, there's so much I should say, but God... I cannot, forgive me, Mother.

Send the teacher to Castiglione, because Sister Anna Gaudenzia lent her to me for eight days. I implore the holy blessing. I kiss your kind hand, your ever

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

For charity's sake, forgive me, because I really cannot write…

55) The Servant of God tells the Mother that she felt great sorrow because she could not write: she tried to do so, but weeping prevented her (Proc. p. 1046).

Palermo, 27 December 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Mother,

My God, what great sorrow I've felt at not being able to write to you… I did write to you, yes, but not even half of what I should have written, and it weighs on me besides, because I addressed it to Rome, but I truly couldn't help it: I'd take up the pen and at once I was forced to weep, seized by a great trembling in my hands, and such confusion in my head that I truly couldn't write anything at all. My God, what I've felt these past days I am not able to explain here. Ah! I beg you, for charity's sake, to forgive me so great and enormous a fault...

Yesterday I telegraphed you, because I truly wish to see you, and speak with you, and accompany you to Palermo.

How are you, Mother? I'd like to tell you so many things, but woe is me, I already feel the usual grief coming over me; what can I do? I really must stop, I can't go on. Forgive me, my Mother, this can be no more than a scrawl. A thousand thanks for the Sisters you're sending me. God reward you. I'll close, prostrate, I implore your Maternal Blessing, your ever

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

56) She asks the Foundress to tell her which sister to put in charge at Sciacca as superior. She will go there at once, taking two sisters with her, and will provisionally give the charge to Sister Anna Fara.

The Servant of God approves what the Mother has done and affirms it is God's will that she reveal everything. She tells her that now she not only may but must go to Palermo, because the devil will do nothing more; it is God's will that she herself accompany her; so she urges her not to stay long in Naples. Further recommendations (Proc. p. 1047).

Palermo, 29 December 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Mother,

I wrote to you yesterday, and today as well, to beg you to tell me whom I should put in as superior at Sciacca, because Sister Anna Geltrude has telegraphed me that both of them have left, and that the girls' parents are complaining, and the thought has come to me that they may have run off?... What wretched creatures, if they've done this... I'm in great distress. My dearest Mother, I wanted to come, because I'd have so much to tell you, but now with this sad news I couldn't come, and tonight I would leave for Sciacca, and I'm bringing Sister Anna Bianchina with me, and could Sister Anna Fara provisionally act as superior?...

Now let's turn to something else. I receive your letter, and hear everything you tell me. Yes; you've done very well, and indeed God wants you to make everything known... and yes, all of it, all of it, will come to pass. Now you may, and must, come to Palermo, because the devil has almost vented all his rage, and can do nothing more, that is, very little... and indeed it must be I who come to accompany you... but come soon, and don't stay long in Naples.

As for Sister Anna Battistina, for charity's sake don't call on her now, because the Commissioner would want only a day to vent his most wicked... and perverse desires; so now I beg you not to move her even for half an hour... As soon as I'm back from Sciacca I'll come myself and tell you everything. In haste, but I beg you to be at peace. Your ever, but

Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

57) She recounts a dream: an eruption of Mount Etna and a great tower that also spewed fire, terrifying the world; frightened, she called upon the Mother, who, together with a religious, was praying, and invited her to pray, and with the prayer the scourge diminished until it ceased.

She asks her to let her know the conditions for opening the house in Terrasini, because they are pressing her about it (Proc. p. 1053).

Palermo, 14 March 1885

Reverend and dearest Mother,

First of all I want to know how you are; I already know you're suffering, and suffering very much; my God, what grief...

My dearest Mother, I would like to tell you a dream, if however you can bear to hear it; otherwise pass over it. I saw as if Etna had caught fire... so that the whole mountain was throwing out great flames, which caused great terror. Then I saw a huge tower, immeasurably wide and tall, and it too was all fire, fire above, fire on the sides, and fire within... so that it terrified most of the world... and I too was filled with fear, and began to cry out: Mother, Mother, Mother, and behold I see a great man coming forward, but I did not recognize him... dressed as a religious; he stood almost beside you, and I was told to pray hard... and both you and that religious began to pray, and made me pray too, and the prayer that had to be said, or was it done? With arms open, in the sign of the cross, and one had to say aloud: My Jesus, mercy... Be moved to pity for your people... Remember we are your handiwork, Jesus, true living God... Ah!... be moved to pity for your suffering people, and in saying these and other prayers the fire diminished, and the great scourge ceased, but slowly. The sky too was like fire, so that it has remained so strongly impressed on me that I still feel myself tremble... and here, in part, is my dream...

Now let's turn to something else. How are you? My God, I fear and know that you're always suffering, good God, what grief. I'll close by asking you to accept the most heartfelt regards of your forever

Most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

I beg you to send the terms for Terrasini soon, because they keep coming every moment to ask for them.

58) Answering some of the Foundress's questions, the Servant of God says she hopes the Father General will not suffer, but the schemes are not yet over; she further states she does not know why he is not yet a cardinal: it is not yet God's will. This she felt so strongly within herself that she had to write it down.

She informs her of the sisters' arrival and will assign them according to the instructions received.

She gives news of the health of other Sisters, and also reports that everyone was very favorably impressed by her visit to Sicily (Proc. p. 1054).

Palermo, 18 March 1885

Reverend and dear Mother,

Here is the continuation of the letter I wrote you; I hope you've received it, and I also hope that the reverend Father General, for now, won't suffer too much, but the schemes are not yet over, no…

Now as to telling you why he must not yet be a cardinal, I really don't know, and why his crown is not yet completed, I really wasn't told; I only said it that way because that's what I felt in my heart, and I had to write it that way because that is what I so strongly felt within me...

Now the Sisters have arrived, so I'll take them at once, as you say, to the Asylum, and the teacher for Linguaglossa I'll take, that is, I'll escort her on Friday, God willing, and I'll go to Castiglione, then I'll take the one you mention, the last one you sent when I was here, in Palermo... Then, on the way back, I'll go to Terranova... and I'll also go to Castelvetrano and Sciacca; I hope to do everything you tell me...

Sister Anna Benedetta asks me to find out which Sister is gravely ill. You know, my Mother, which one it is... it's the last one who came when you were here, the one from Altamura, who came from Piacenza, whom Sister Anna Celsa put to bed because she was swollen, so she hasn't gotten up since; the doctor comes every day, she coughs up blood and has a continuous fever...

The one who came from Adernò, that is Sister Anna Demetria, is up, but not doing well at all... The one who came from Castelvetrano also has a bad cough... but is still up... they take cod liver oil and a decoction of cinchona bark, as does Sister Anna Gemma.

Now I would ask you, dear Mother, out of charity, to tell me which Sister I should leave in my place, because once you told me not to leave Sister Anna Paolina in charge again. I'll try to do this quickly, but I won't be able to be home for five or six days...

Now let's turn to something else. You ask me whether I still cry? Dear Mother, these are my virtues... Lauretta is a little better; indeed she sends you a million greetings and always remembers you, and asks me: How is the Mother? Now let's turn to you, dear Mother, how are you? My God, who knows how much you suffer... My Mother, you can't imagine the great emptiness you left behind; my God, I can't bear to think of it… You can't imagine the great and beautiful impression you made on everyone who had the good fortune to see you...

Yesterday Maria Teresa came, and told me that the Mother has wounded her heart, but she was forced to do so to calm her Mama, but that now she finds herself very worried. The Princess sends her a thousand regards. I hope the dear children are well, as is the lady Countess.

I'd like to tell you so many other things, but I'd like the letter to be able to go off.

Please accept my most heartfelt regards, while I beg you to say many things on my behalf also to the distinguished Mr. Checco... I beg your maternal blessing, while I have the good fortune of being also your

Most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

I'm sending you a ticket you wanted, for the railways.

59) Having visited the houses of Sciacca and Castelvetrano, according to her instructions, the Servant of God is now ready to leave to give her account in person.

She felt enormous sorrow because, during her absence, Sister Anna Romualda died (Proc. p. 1058).

Palermo, 12 April 1885

A. M. F.

Reverend and dear Mother,

Here I am back in Palermo. I went to Sciacca and to Castelvetrano, as you told me to... As for Sciacca, it's truly a lovely and dear Community, and then whenever you tell me to come I'll come at once, at the merest sign from you, because the visits you had ordered me to make, by God's grace, I made. I have only one great sorrow, which really torments me, and it is this: that on returning home I found poor Sister Anna Romualda dead... My God, what sharp grief I felt, my Mother... good God played a trick on me, letting me go out and then taking the Sister. Enough, I hope you'll forgive me, won't you, dear Mother?... I truly hoped to get back in time, but good God allowed me to have this sharp grief... It's only fair, for so many misdeeds of mine…

Now I beg you, out of charity, to tell me whether I should come, even by telegram, because before I really couldn't. I'll give you the account of the Houses in person, because it will be better...

Now I beg you to tell me whether I should wait for a postulant to enter, provided you're not in a hurry to leave for Piacenza... because if you're in a hurry, then I'll come at once and alone, since that postulant hasn't entered yet; I would be glad, because she has a thousand francs, so with a little of my own... and 500 from the house in Sciacca, though it's always a small thing, but which my fancy would like to bring you...

Now let's turn to something else. Dear Mother, you asked me in your letter whether I should leave Sister Anna Corinna in charge? Well, I haven't left her, because I had no order to do so, but if you wish it, I'll gladly leave her... I await your answer on how to proceed...

I'll close by asking you to accept the most heartfelt regards, while, prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing and forgiveness for every fault of mine, while I have the happy fortune of being also your

Most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

60) Parting from the Mother was very hard for her, especially because she found her ill. She writes that they will offer special prayers to obtain the grace she desires, and is certain of obtaining it. She expresses feelings of great affection and much gratitude (Proc. p. 1059).

[Palermo], 23 April 1885

A. M. F.

My dear Mother,

How hard this parting was, that is, having to leave you so, ill… My God, I truly cannot explain it, I felt my heart being torn apart. Ah! Oh dear Mother, how much you suffer, and all for what? For our wickedness and bad conduct. My God, what sharp grief. Enough, only good God can give you strength to suffer all that you suffer, oh dear Mother.

Now we've begun a strong novena to dear Our Lady and to Jesus in the Sacrament, and I hope you'll obtain the grace, and now I'd like to be mistress of the whole world, because I'd like to spend it all on you alone… after God, Mo[ther], you, you, and we all wish you every good... On Sunday, God willing, we'll also have adoration, and it will all be for you, dear Mother, and then so many other prayers... My God, how glad I'll be when you've received what you desire, and I already consider it certain...

Now how are you? I always seem to see you so suffering… And the lady Countess, how is she? My God, what grief I felt at leaving without saying goodbye to her. I know the dear children are well. I beg you to accept so many greetings from Father Briuccia, who, on reading your note, was so pleased I cannot explain it; the nuns too, his sisters, send you so many greetings…

I'll close, so as not to trouble you further, while, prostrate, I implore your maternal blessing and forgiveness for every fault of mine. My God, when I think of the happy fortune I have of being also among your Daughters, my heart fills with holy joy. Ah!... how could I ever show my gratitude, oh dear Mother? A thousand lives would not be enough… Please accept the most sincere regards of your

Most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

61) Having been gravely ill for a month, the Servant of God has not been able to write. The pains, which never leave her, prevent her from carrying out her duty. She thanks the Mother for her prayers.

As for Sister Anna Colomba, she believes it to be a slander, since on every occasion she praises the Mother and the Institute (Proc. p. 1060).

Palermo, 27 May 1885

A.M.F.

Reverend Mother,

Having been gravely ill for more than a month, I was never able to write to you, and now, tormented as before by the same pains, which leave me neither by day nor by night and do not allow me, much to my sorrow, to carry out the obligations I am bound to, that is, to give you, my good Mother, an account of all that is presently happening. But I assure you that as soon as I can hold the pen in my hand I shall not fail to give you a full account of everything. I thank you, then, for your concern for me and for the prayer you offer to God for my poor health; ah, keep it up, for charity's sake, for I have great need of it.

Know that I have received all your letters, even the registered one. As for what you tell me about Sister Anna Colomba, so far I have absolutely nothing to complain of; she behaves very well, and I have found no fault in her at all; I believe it to be, rather, a great slander. When she came to Palermo she asked to see Monsignor Cerino, and I, knowing nothing about the sister, sent her with Sister Anna Macrina, and she did nothing but praise you and the Institute, so much so that Monsignor was most pleased and satisfied.

Then her father came to see her, to tell her that her mother was gravely ill, and I gave her leave once more; she went with her sister, and amid so many people who came to see her she did nothing but praise you and the Institute. What do you make of that? And then she said: Ah, if I had to make another journey with Ruffina I would really wear myself out.

I ask you, with all my heart, for the holy blessing, together with all the sisters, and I remain always your

Most affectionate daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

62) It was a suffering for the Servant of God not to be able to write to the Mother: the fever and the pains gave her no respite.

She is very grieved at the Count's behavior toward Carlotta.

She assures her there will be no cholera: the Foundress's sufferings and sacrifices keep God's punishments at bay.

She thanks her for having given her the obedience to be cured, and for the prayers she has offered for her (Proc. p. 1062).

Palermo, 28 May 1885

A. M. F.

Ever dearest Mother,

My God, what sharp grief I felt at not being able to write to you, and I couldn't even read your letters, so dear to me, because the high fever and such sharp pains really didn't let me put two words together.

Now let's leave that and turn to something else. I read your registered letter, and I'm most grieved over that Count, who truly makes a martyr of that dear creature; my God, what grief I feel, especially since she finds herself in that position, it's truly a great sorrow, and my thought, after you, dear Mother, is always for Lady Carlotta...

Now let's turn to something else. As for what you ask me, whether cholera, or some other contagious illness, will come, it seems to me it will not, for this year. But do you know who holds back the divine arm so much? Your sacrifices, your sufferings, in short, the great good you, oh dear Mother, do in this spoiled and ruined world.

Mother, ah!... oh my Mother, ah!... I beg you to forgive me if I have behaved so badly toward you, who, after God, have been and are my greatest benefactress. Because if I have the great good fortune to find myself in the House of God, it is all owing to your great goodness.

Mother, I'd like to tell you so many things, but my hand trembles so much I really cannot. For charity's sake, I beg you to be at ease, nothing else will happen...

Ah!... may good God reward you, oh Mother, for your great kindness in giving me the obedience to be cured, and for the great prayers you offered for me, which I shall truly never be able to forget... I'll write to you tomorrow.

Please accept the most heartfelt regards of your

Most Unworthy Daughter

Sister Anna del Salvatore

Forgive me.

63) This letter fragment contains prophecies — largely fulfilled — concerning the Foundress: she will die in Rome, her body will remain incorrupt, she will be buried not in the Verano cemetery, but among her daughters; many will come to ask for graces; later she will be placed among the founders in St. Peter's.

Rosa Gattorno did indeed die in Rome, and was buried in the Verano cemetery, but her body was later translated to the church attached to the Generalate (1932), and has remained incorrupt.

On 9 April 2000 she was beatified in St. Peter's Square together with 4 other Servants of God (Proc. p. 1086).

[Palermo, March-May 1885?]

A. M. F.

Reverend Mother,

Right now I'd like to explain myself here by telling you something, and it is that you, my Mother, will die, if I'm not mistaken, you will die in Rome, and your body will not be corrupted, so that the worms will have nothing to do with it; and then you will not be buried at San Lorenzo, but we shall have the good fortune to keep you with us… The great crowds will come to obtain graces, and they will obtain them... afterward you will be placed among the founders, in St. Peter's. Ah!... how fitting that will be.

Now let's turn to something else. As for your graces, that is, your three… yes, notable graces, they will be granted to you, but not for now, no, you won't be able to receive them that way […]

b) Letters to Some Sisters

Among the letters chosen, 6 are addressed to Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega.

With the simplicity that is natural to her, the Servant of God addresses the recipients of her letters with such affection and care, informing them of particular situations, expressing her gratitude for the good example she has received; offering her remembrance in prayer; sharing spiritual experiences, confirming her readiness to help, showing all of them her feelings of kindness and humility.

1) Writing to the Superior, who has just left, the Servant of God rejoices that the journey went well; she expresses sorrow at the separation but confirms her readiness to obey. She also gives an account of the house (Proc. p. 717).

[Sampierdarena, March 1873]

A. M. F.

S B L G N M S A M D Imm.ta [Blessed be our glorious Mother St. Anne, mother of the Immaculate]

La B D N E P S C noi [May the blessing of our Eternal Father be with us]

Most beloved Superior,

I received your dear letter, which brought me so much, so much joy, my dear Superior, to hear that you had a good journey and that you're well; and I hope the Lord will let the Rome journey go well too, but it grieves me that I no longer see you... wherever I look for you I no longer see you at all...

Every time I go to my room I remember those words you used to say to me, and I shall always hold them dear... truly, my good Superior... I pray and have others pray; the little girls study, always longing for their beloved Superior. The sisters keep asking me: When will our Superior come? For me it's like a continual martyrdom, my dear, patience... I'm ready to do everything you've told me. So long as it pleases my God and my dear Mother, and you... and Mother St. Anne.

Good Superior, tell dear Mother I'm ready to do whatever she commands, and though incapable, God can do anything. Dear Superior, come soon. Sister Anna Giulia asks me to tell you to greet the Mother on her behalf, and to tell you not to forget that she will not forget you.

My Superior, Patelani is very poorly, I now have hardly any hope left. The little girl with the eye problem is still the same. The Vernengo Sisters ask me in my room, they told me that on St. Joseph's day, from morning until evening, they would hold the exposition, and I told them as you told me to tell them, and then they did it, but at their own expense.

I'd have so many things to tell you, but time is short because I'm keeping the night watch over Patelani, who is poorly. Tell the Mother to bless her... My dear Superior, I don't know whether you've understood me, forgive me, I don't know whether you've understood.

Please accept my most distinguished regards, and those of all the dear sisters and your little girls; come soon, come soon, dear one… I beg you, for charity's sake, to forgive my scribblings. Please greet the Mother for me, and Sister Anna Vincenza, and little Carlotta. Farewell, my good Superior. Farewell.

I am your most affectionate Sister

Sister Anna del Salvatore
