2) The Servant of God informs the Superior of a neighboring Community that the postulants will arrive without their dowry, because she has sent the money to the Foundress in Rome; she also says she has kept some sheets because she needed them.

She asks for news of Sister Anna Gabriella and Sister Anna Corinna (Proc. p. 797).

Florence, 17 May 1877

A. M. F.

My dearest and beloved Superior,

Two hurried lines to tell you that the two postulants are coming without a dowry, because the Mother wrote to me from Rome that I should accept that postulant who had already been accepted by her, and that I should send the money to her in Rome because she needed it; so I sent it to her, and indeed I was even confused, because I thought I had kept back the fare money, but instead I was left with only ten lire. But this dowry was very small, because one, that is Leonilde's, didn't come to a hundred francs, and the other's a little more. So you can imagine what a large sum the dear Mother must have received.

My good and beloved Superior, I beg you to forgive me if I'm taking too much advantage of your Goodness, because I kept four sheets, since I didn't know what to put on the beds; I've already told the Mother about this, but if she isn't pleased it would grieve me, even though they're only two-panel ones, the thickest only…

The Sisters are well, they send you a thousand greetings; of myself I'll say nothing, only that I feel a slow fever in my bones that is wearing away my life. And how are you? Do you still keep martyring that poor little body of yours? How gladly I would see you, and how gladly I would give you a kiss... How is Sister Anna Gabriella? Tell her that for St. Anne's feast, if I'm still alive, I'll bring her a lovely lemon plant. How is Sister Anna Corinna? Her Brother wants letters from her, Pietro as well as the other one and the sister-in-law; indeed he complains that she never writes to them, especially the latter, I say "the latter" because I don't know his name.

I'll close these scribblings of mine by asking your forgiveness for every fault of mine.

Please accept my most sincere regards, while, with distinguished esteem, I have the honor to style myself

Your most lowly Sister

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

I beg a prayer for me to Jesus, for charity's sake… I'm handing you the certificates for both of them. It seems to me the linen-keeper kept 44 ells of cloth and 4 petticoats; this is Nonziata's and Leonilde's. Sheets: 4.

3) She expresses a keen desire to see Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega again, and tells her that during her stay in Florence, Carlotta was very well; so too her little daughter.

She then expresses admiration for Sister Anna Benedetta's virtues, and feelings of humility (Proc. p. 801).

Florence, 30 May 1877

A. M. F.

Reverend and good Sister Anna Benedetta,

How grateful I was for your dear and thoughtful letter, I cannot explain to you here... only my poor heart can know it. Ah, how gladly I would see you, how many beautiful things I would like to tell you, it seems to me a thousand and a thousand years since I last saw you. Ah, how gladly I would give you a kiss, ah, how gladly I would say some little word to you!…

You ask me: what impression did little Carlotta make on me? My God, what sorrow... it brought me to tears... but in that short time she stayed here in Florence she was very well and didn't even cough, because Count Gaspare told me that in Rome she had much more of it; as for the little girl, how well she was, words can't say more; and then we remembered you so much, dear Sister Anna Benedetta.

The Mother has arrived in Piacenza and in two days I'll go there too. I hope you have received the Sisters' things; I asked the linen-keeper to send you everything, but I don't know whether it all got there; should something happen to be missing, let me know and I'll send it to you at once. I'll close these scribblings of mine by asking your forgiveness for every fault of mine. Please accept my most distinguished regards; I beg you to share them with the good Sisters, and in particular with Sister Anna Rosa.

I beg you to breathe a sigh for me to Jesus, because you are so rich in merits and so full of every virtue with the deepest humility... whereby you draw down upon yourself and upon the whole Institute the choicest blessings... Ah yes, with all your heroic virtues you make our Institute prosper... But I rejoice that the Most High Lord will reward you generously, and will let fall upon your head the dew of His Love and will fill you with the choicest graces. I beg you to forgive my errors, while I style myself your

Most Unworthy Servant

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

4) The Servant of God expresses affection and submission, reminding Sister Anna Benedetta that the house of Florence must be dear to her, because it was the first one she founded.

She asks for clarification about the bonnets she is to buy; she will send Sister Anna Assunta's linen (Proc. p. 817).

Florence, 27 October 1877

A. M. F.

Dear and good Sister Anna Benedetta,

Two lines to thank you for the kindness you show us in remembering me and all of us poor little ones here in Florence. Ah yes, dear Sister Anna Benedetta, after the Reverend and dear Mother, you alone are the dearest to us... and all of us, after the dear Mother, will pray for you, because this house must be the dearest to you, since it was your first house, which you founded. Just as for the dear Mother it will be the dearest because it gives her the most to worry about, so too for you, because perhaps we don't do what we ought to do; and I most of all, because I'm the one who gives the dear Mother the most grief, and without even realizing it.

I'll send Sister Anna Assunta's linen as you tell me, because I meant to send it the other day by the carrier; so I've put it off until Monday; the wine still hasn't arrived...

Good Sister Anna Benedetta, as for what you tell me about doing everything well, I promise you that as far as my poor capacity will reach, I am ready to obey you.

As for the bonnets, you don't tell me whether they're the woolen kind, or the white kind, because I went there, I and Sister Anna Giuseppina, and she told me she didn't remember what they were like, and the merchant told me he hadn't taken in any bonnets of any sort... Send me word how and where, and I'll dispatch them at once. I've sent some vegetables to the dear Mother, with a little bit of Dutch cheese, for her to try; if she likes it I'll send her more.

Please accept my regards, and those of all the Sisters, who love you so much, while

I remain your unworthy Sister

Sister Anna del Salvatore

5) With very affectionate expressions, she asks for news of Sister Anna Letizia and of other sisters of the Appignano community.

She reports that she is together with her sister Sister Anna Fabiana, in a newly opened house. She sends greetings to the Parish Priest and to other benefactresses (Proc. p. 857).

Rome, 14 November 1878

A. M. F.

Beloved Sister [Sister Anna Letizia Sordi],

My Letizia, if I may still call you so... Tell me, my dear, how are you? Ah, how often, how often you come to my mind!... Mine forever, I would wish for a letter from you, because I fear you're not well; poor thing, who knows how much you suffer, it seems to me I see you, yes, it seems I hear you with that nasty cough… Ah, dearest, how great is my grief!...

Good Sister Anna Letizia, I'm now with my Sister, Sister Anna Fabiana, in a new house: the poor thing always remembers you, we always talk about you… Tell me, please tell me who your Superior is, because I would like to know her. How is poor Sister Anna Corinna? Is Sister Anna Beniamina well? And does good Sister Anna Pacifica still keep sighing? What is Sister Anna Natalina doing with her looms? Have they forgotten poor Sister Anna del Salvatore? Yes, surely they have forgotten, haven't they? Not I, truly not, and Sister Anna Letizia doesn't forget me either, poor thing, does she? Sister Anna Fabiana tells me to send you ever so many things.

How is Mrs. Rita? Say so many things to her for me. And is Mrs. Lui well? Say so many things to her for me, tell her I'll never forget the great good she did me, especially how much she suffered for me when, out of her kindness, she accompanied me to Loreto in that weather, poor thing!...

Please say so many things for me to the most reverend Parish Priest, tell him, I beg you, to commend me to Jesus, as I always commend him every day at Holy Communion; but I beg you, for charity's sake, not to say where I am; if you love me you'll do it, won't you? My dear, mine... my Letizia, tell me, how is your dear mother? Has it been long since you've had news of her? Poor thing!...

My beloved, I must close because my duties are so many you could never believe it!... I don't know whether you received a letter of mine written on the journey... I leave you with the hope of seeing you again... please say so many things for me to the good Sisters, and you, my good Sister Anna Letizia, receive a thousand ki[sses]... and a warm embrace in the Heart of Jesus, from your

Your unworthy Sister

Sister Anna del Salvatore

My Address is Vicolo Riari No. 43

Shelter of St. Mary Magdalene

6) She has received the fellow sister's note and tells her she will pass the request on to Maria Teresa, but she already feels in her heart that the answer will be affirmative.

She affirms that it is no pride to wish to know whether Our Lady loves us, because Our Lady wants us to turn to her with great trust (Proc. p.1023).

Palermo, 15 June 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Sister Anna Benedetta,

I receive with the greatest pleasure your unexpected little note, which took me quite by surprise; and that very night I made my Holy Communion together with you... and it struck me deeply, not knowing why you were telling me to pray and pray hard. Do you know what night it was? It was Friday night, the 13th. Enough, I can't tell you everything here.

As for what you tell me to say to Maria Teresa, who would like to know whether the Most Holy Virgin loves her... yes, as soon as I can see her I'll ask her... and then I'll write and tell you what she says... But I already feel in my heart that she loves her... and greatly loves her, and she herself will see it...

Do you say you're afraid it's too much pride to ask the Most Holy Virgin whether she loves you? Ah! no, on the contrary, Our Lady is pleased that we come to her with trust, and is immensely consoled that we hold her as our Mother, entirely our own... Dear Mary, most beautiful Mary. But… I'd like to tell you so many things, but my mind is a little confused right now. I'll write when I've spoken with Maria Teresa...

I beg you to forgive all my errors, while I ask you to accept the most heartfelt regards and a million thanks from the Sisters for the lovely holy cards you sent them; they always remember you and long to see you soon, you and the dearest Mother. I would ask you to offer my most heartfelt regards to the lady Countess Carlotta and to Sister Anna Celsa, and please accept a million of the most heartfelt regards from your

Unworthy Sister

Sister Anna del Salvatore

7) She thanks the superior Sister Anna della Mercede for having sent the accounts promptly: she will also inform the Mother.

She then humbly asks not to be given the title of Provincial any longer; she also informs her of the holy death of Sister Anna Francesca Savignone [niece of the Foundress] (Proc. p. 1027).

Palermo, 28 July 1884

A. M. F.

Dearest Superior [Sister Anna della Mercede],

I have received your dear letter, with the half-year's statement and the money order for 400 lire. Well done, Superior, what great care you took; may good God reward you by granting you every grace your so generous and kind heart could desire... Now I'll also write to the reverend Mother to say how prompt you've been...

Now let's turn to ourselves. How are you? Always suffering, aren't you? My God, what great grief your health causes me, you cannot believe it… Dear Superior of God's heart, I would like to ask you a great favor, and it is this: do not call me Provincial any longer; ah!... for pity's sake, I beg you not to give me that so sad a name... for me... for, being so good as you are, I am most certain and sure you will want to console me... won't you?

Now I give you the sad news about dear Sister Anna Francesca, who died on 24 June, as Sister Anna Celsa wrote to tell me, and the dear Mother also wrote to tell me she had a most beautiful death… and the reverend Mother attended her... what good fortune, what a beautiful death...

Now I'll close, for I'm afraid of boring you with my scribblings; enough, you, being so good, will forgive my great blunders and errors. Please accept, most beloved Superior, the most heartfelt regards from me and from all the Sisters, while I thank you again for the promptness with which you sent me the accounts…. Yes, the reverend Mother too will be very pleased…. Please accept once more my most heartfelt regards, while I give you a warm embrace in the sweet heart of Jesus, your

Unworthy Sister

Sister Anna del Salvatore

8) She answers Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega's letter and questions: the sufferings she feels are a grace from Jesus, and what she does for the Mother is pleasing to Him.

She affirms that the Foundress's brothers will be saved for the good they have done for the Institute; the Virgin will protect their family members too.

She assures her that she will become a saint and will go on helping the Mother and the Institute for a long time yet (Proc. p. 1037).

Palermo, 3 October 1884

A. M. F.

Reverend and dearest Sister Anna Benedetta,

I have received a letter from you so dear to me, and here I am ready to answer everything you ask me, with such humility, that is, to pray. Yes, I promise you, though you have no need of my prayers, because it is your humility that makes you say all this; but I can assure you that Jesus loves you very much, and that the afflictions you feel are one of the most beautiful graces that good God pours into your heart, to make you ever richer in merit; and you, better than I, know that good God makes all His most beloved souls suffer more than all the rest. Ah!... fortunate and a thousand times happy are you, of whom, every day or almost every day, the Lord asks the most beautiful gift a loving soul can ever offer Him, which are inward sorrows, the most agonizing, but the most meritorious...

As for the dear Mother, you know very well her goodness and generosity, so don't think about that at all, because what she does is out of the great love she bears the dearest Mother; so it is not at all displeasing to Jesus, on the contrary, it is a generosity of souls that the Lord leads to great holiness... Yes... she will become a saint...

As for the dear Mother's brothers, solely for the great good they have done and continue to do for the Institute, good God will save them. Yes, He will save them; and if my prayers are worth anything, after the dear Mother, we will pray for their salvation, for I well know both you and the reverend Mother desire it... and I truly hope the Most Holy Virgin will grant these graces... So too you tell me about your own brothers and sisters; well, the Most Holy Virgin will watch over them too... fear nothing, for good God will pour out great blessings.

I would like to tell you so many things, but my very small capacity does not allow me to explain them here; I only beg you to be cheerful and content, because your place is among the Saints, and you will long help our dear Mother and the Institute…

I'll close my scribblings by asking your forgiveness for every fault of mine; please accept the most heartfelt regards of your

Unworthy Sister

Sister Anna del Salvatore

9) She answers Sister Anna Benedetta again with deep humility: only her goodness sees anything good in her, acknowledging that it is only through God's mercy, the Mother's kindness, and the sisters' charity that she is allowed to remain in community.

She also thanks her and the Mother for the good they have done for the Community (Proc. p. 1050).

Palermo, 17 February 1885

Dearest Sister Anna Benedetta,

I receive your letter, so dear to me, which you wrote with such kindness... and without my deserving it; no, truly, I did not deserve it, no...

And then everything you say… I have really done nothing, nothing, only your great kindness, which accepts everything, but ah!.. for charity's sake, I beg you not to use such expressions with me: that I have shown you charity and kindness.... Ah!.. I repeat, for charity's sake, never say that to me again, for I know all too well I haven't done what I should have done... And then, that I have a good heart? My God, my heart… is worse than a tigress, and is a volcano full of every iniquity, that is what my heart is... And then, that I have virtues… Good God, what confusion such words cause me!... I know you say this for my own good, and so that I might come to that point which, in all your kindness, you tell me of.

It is only through the great mercy of good God and the very great kindness of our dear Mother that I have been brought to this point, to be able to live in community, and through the kindness of the Sisters who so charitably bear with me; for the rest, I am nothing but an abyss of iniquity… and I fear I am, and am, the disgrace of heaven and earth.

Now let's turn to something else. I hear the dear Mother has suffered greatly; my God, what sorrow… I hear of so many kind attentions and the fine care Mr. Checco has taken: may good God reward him, pouring down upon him, his children, and his wife every greatest good with all the choicest prosperity....

Yes, please accept, oh dear Sister Anna Benedetta, a thousand thanks for the great good you have done for me, and for this Community, and I beg you to thank the dearest Mother on my behalf for so much good and charity she has shown us; I shall never be able to forget it. Ah, the great good she has done for this House.... God, what an emptiness they have left... I cannot explain it here.

Please accept the most heartfelt regards from me and from all the sisters

Your Unworthy Sister

Sister Anna del Salvatore

10) The Servant of God feels great sorrow over the Mother's illness, caused by so much toil and grief. To her she attributes the warding off of God's punishments, and for her capacity for suffering calls her a heroine and precious gem of God's heart.

She foresees that the Mother will have many more years of life and strength yet, to suffer and to merit (Proc. p. 1051).

Palermo, 28 February 1885

Dearest Sister Anna Benedetta,

God, what sharp grief on learning, from your telegram, that the dear Mother is unwell... and running a high fever. Ah!... for charity's sake, how did this happen? What has happened?

I already seem to hear it repeated... the great toils, exhaustion, and continual sacrifices and sorrows always and without respite... And here is the illness of our dear Mother, the dearest one now on earth, the one who makes reparation for so many of God's punishments that would fall upon us, were it not for our dearest Mother... yes, it is she who, through her continual martyrdoms, gives us life of soul and health of body; yes, it is she who, through her continual and serious illnesses, is, is, is... a shield against so many scourges that would fall upon wretched humanity....

Ah!... oh dearest Sister Anna Benedetta, beloved joy of God's heart, how much good that Heroine, the precious Gem of God's Heart, our dear Mother, does even in her suffering… Good God will surely give her yet many years of life and strength, ever more to suffer and to merit... I would never finish if I tried to say, even in part, how great our holy Mother is... I beg you, oh dearest Sister Anna Benedetta, say so many things to her for me, and that I shall never, never ever forget the great good she has done for me and for this Community.

Now let's turn to you. How is your health? How do you feel? My God, who knows how much you too suffer... both for yourself and for seeing the dear Mother suffer so much… For charity's sake, take care of yourself, and love Jesus very, very much, also for me, who do not know how to love… What an emptiness they have left!... what a loss that departure was.... enough, I don't want to bore you any further with my scribblings. I wish you every good and every heavenly consolation and all those lovely gifts your most generous heart desires… Please accept the most heartfelt regards of your forever

Most Unworthy Servant

Sister Anna del Salvatore

I beg you to forgive the great many errors.

Postscript. The Sister who fell ill is still poorly, indeed today she is gravely so...

11) She thanks Sister Anna Celsa Speranza for writing to her; the days of the visit were, for her, holy days, in which she received only good example.

She also asks her to thank the Mother for the good she has done the community (Proc. p. 1086).

[Palermo, February-March 1885]

Good and dear Sister Anna Celsa,

I thank you for your kindness in writing to me, in which you thank me for my attentions and ask forgiveness for the scandals given. Ah!.. oh God, we have received nothing else but good and holy example.

Yes, I can assure you that for all of us they were holy days, days of great edification; and indeed I beg you, for charity's sake, to forgive me the little attention I paid you. My God, how it grieves me; may good God reward you for the good you have done us poor little ones.

I truly cannot find peace, having passed those lovely days without profiting from so very many good examples and so many virtues. I assure you it was, for me and for all of us, a great school, and the lessons shall never be erased. I beg you to thank the dear Mother on my behalf for having deigned to stay in this house, to which she brought every good. Ah!.. the great good the dear Mother has done this community. The Sisters always remember her, and she is always on their lips.

I bid you farewell, for the post is leaving and I can write no more

Your Unworthy Sister

Sister Anna del Salvatore

I'll write to you tomorrow.

c) Letters to Other People

Of these letters, one is addressed to Father Cusmano, now Blessed; 3 are written to Carlotta Custo, the Foundress's deaf-mute daughter.

Though aware of her limited education, somewhat awkward and perhaps intimidated when addressing people she regards as distinguished, the Servant of God never fails to convey the delicacy of her spirit, expressing her thoughts with sincere concern for the problems of those she comes into contact with.

1) She informs Father Cusmano that, the present premises no longer being sufficient, she is about to move into the rooms made available by Msgr. Briuccia in his palace. By agreement with Archbishop Msgr. Celesia, they will nevertheless still continue to make use of his house (Proc. p. 930).

Palermo, 26 February 1882

A. M. F.

Reverend Father Cusmano,

I feel it my duty to inform you that the Reverend Father Briuccia has made over a room to us in his palace. We have accepted it, and within a few days we will go to take up residence there.

Monsignor the Archbishop has cooperated in this; and meanwhile, by his wise counsel, we are obliged to retain this House, because the new one does not meet all the needs of the Community, which is beginning to grow numerous.

I hastened to pass this news on to you, because I know how much interest you take in the affairs of our poor Institute. Asking for your holy blessing, I remain of Your Reverence

Most lowly servant

Sister Anna del Salvatore

2) Writing to the Foundress's daughter, Carlotta Custo, the Servant of God rejoices over her little daughter's recovery and attributes it to the Mother's prayers and sufferings. She offers good wishes for the Christmas feasts, also on behalf of the community (Proc. p. 1001).

Palermo, 20 December 1883

Most esteemed Lady Countess,

I feel the need to share my joy over dear little Noni's recovered health. Ah!.. how dear she is to Mary.... I imagine the great sorrow you, most kind Lady Countess, must have felt in those days... My God!... it seemed to me I saw you so grieved that even my own heart could bear it no longer... enough. Now it is all over, because the dear Mother has obtained from the Most Holy Virgin the long-hoped-for grace of her recovery, and she will be well...

Here too we prayed and had others pray... but it was our reverend and dear Mother who obtained the grace. Yes, the great sacrifices she makes and the great sufferings she bears are able to obtain from God the most notable graces...

I make this known to you through this letter, certain that you will accept these expressions of mine.

I take, then, this happy occasion to wish you a most joyous coming Christmas season and the start of the year about to begin, with the wish that you and your whole distinguished Family may complete it happily. Please accept the good wishes the whole community sends you, for your prosperity and that of your respected Family, while, with all affection, your

Unworthy servant

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

I ask forgiveness for every fault of mine

3) She answers Countess Carlotta's letter: she assures her that her family is specially protected by the Most Holy Virgin (Proc. p. 1032).

Palermo, 19 August 1884

A. M. F.

Most Illustrious Lady Countess,

First of all I prostrate myself at your feet, begging you to forgive me so grave a fault, for not having answered your so delicate and kind letter at once.

Now here I am, ready to tell Your Most Illustrious Ladyship, and to beg you to be cheerful and content; for charity's sake, do so, for that is what the Most Holy Virgin wishes. She sends you this affliction because she loves you dearly, and I know, alas, your afflictions, but take heart and fear nothing, for both you and your whole illustrious and noble family are so regarded with an eye of special favor by the Most Holy Virgin, that it is truly impossible to explain it here. I am therefore right to tell you to be cheerful and content, and that Jesus will pour the choicest blessings upon your so chosen and privileged family... So take heart, for your afflictions will serve you as a great crown in heaven and a great honor on this earth…

I can assure you that, if I could, I would give my life a thousand times over to ease your afflictions, but good God wills it so... I am glad the dearest children are well and will remain well... for they are very well watched over and cared for by the Virgin, who will therefore keep them from every danger, even from this so terrible scourge.

For now I won't dwell any longer on my scribblings, but I repeat, be cheerful, for one so privileged as Your Illustrious Ladyship is not found, and will not be found, among a thousand. Oh!... fair and fortunate... C…

I, though most unworthy, pray and shall pray; and if Jesus accepts it, I assure you that you will have the greatest consolations…

I beg you to accept my most sincere and profound regards, while, with all affection, I wish you every most abundant good... prosperity, health, and peace and riches in plenty... I give a warm embrace to the dearest children and a warm kiss to Your Illustrious Ladyship. Ever your

Unworthy Servant

Sister Anna del Salvatore

4) She has received the Countess's letter; she promises her own prayers and assures her of the Virgin's love (Proc. p. 1035).

Palermo, 17 September 1884

A. M. F.

Most Illustrious Lady Countess

I have just received your most esteemed letter. Oh! how it pleased me, I really cannot explain it in words. I shall raise to good God the most fervent prayers... not I alone, but the whole entire community, that good God may console you always, always, and grant you the choicest graces.

I am most glad that the dearest children are well. I am only most grieved that Your Illustrious Ladyship is not well; my God, what great sorrow my heart feels. Ah!... for charity's sake, take care of yourself, because your health is too necessary and too valuable…

As for what Your Illustrious Ladyship tells me, for now I still cannot say anything, because many more prayers are still needed; so let us pray for now, and then you will do what your most generous heart tells you. Most Holy Mary loves you very much, and so she will console you, granting your prayer and all those consolations and joys Your Illustrious Ladyship could desire: prosperity, health and peace, with the greatest riches… in short, every consolation that so noble a heart deserves; and I shall never be content, nor shall I stop praying, until I see you content and consoled.

Yes, these are my vows, these my wishes, these my prayers, which I offer night and morning and always...

I'll close my scribblings, begging you to forgive every fault of mine, while, with the highest and most distinguished esteem, I remain of Your Most Illustrious Ladyship

Faithful Servant

Sister Anna del Salvatore

I beg you to forgive me for having had to write to you, out of necessity, on this half sheet. I give a warm kiss to dearest Nonni, and a little caress to Nini.

Presented under this heading are the Opinions of the theological Censors on the writings of the Servant of God, and the Report of the historical Experts on the documentary research carried out.

1. Opinion of the Most Reverend Prof. Don Rosario La Delfa, first theological Censor of the writings of the Servant of God, dated 13 April 1999 (Proc. pp. 435-439).

Having read and attentively examined the letters of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, which were entrusted to me for an assessment of their value in relation to the faith expressed therein and to the personality of the Servant of God, I declare first of all that nowhere in these writings is there to be found any element that, manifestly or covertly, is prejudicial or opposed to the Catholic faith, and that every principle expressed in them and every action described is not contrary to good morals.

I am, on the other hand, pleased to note how greatly the notions brought out by these writings contribute

1) to confirm the esteem for the personality of the Servant of God;

2) to enrich the patrimony of the faith itself;

3) to ascertain the high degree of theological life expressed in the exercise of certain Christian virtues.

a) Personality

From a reading of the letters there emerges immediately, and with impressive consistency, a clear and open character, surrounded by a rare blend of optimism and realism. This trait of her personality is evident in her serene view of daily life, and can be most accurately gauged from her unconditional embrace of the duties of her state, especially in the boundless sensitivity she showed toward the Institute to which she belonged and its Rule, toward the other sisters entrusted to her, toward the Foundress Mother, toward the sick both poor and rich alike, toward benefactors, and toward other people who pass through the scene of her mission (for example, young girls, priests and bishops).

Clearly apparent are the total giving of herself to the point of exhausting her physical strength, and a heroic submission of her own reasoning and feelings to the mission gradually entrusted to her. Yet always present is a surprising sense of evangelical optimism, which can be amply observed in the constancy of her human attitude in the face of various circumstances, even the most difficult; in her conviction of the perfectibility of plans; in the expectations she placed in other people; in the good humor that frequently shows through in some of her expressions of wonder.

b) Faith

Reading the letters in chronological progression, three stages can be identified in the growth of this virtue in relation to the various moments of the Servant of God's Christian and apostolic growth. The first stage concerns the expression of faith as abandonment to providence. This matures in a second moment, defined by recourse to unceasing prayer. The letters of the final period of her earthly existence show a unitive stage of the Servant of God with God and the Church.

From the first period examined are the letters in which the affirmations of faith appear as expectancy and abandonment in God. Before the work of God, the Servant of God can only show amazement. This amazement nourishes expectancy, that is, the certainty that God himself will make the works of the Institute flourish. Providence, however, is not to be identified with an ex machina intervention of God: it manifests itself as a divine pedagogy that purifies within a final, otherworldly perspective. The ideal expressed by firm faith in providence becomes the measure of reality, understood as the concrete and ever-inadequate earthly situation, and constitutes the motive for a longing for abandonment in spiritual and bodily activities that can improve the conditions of the world and dispose it toward God.

The growing awareness that works of mercy bring a positive outcome to the mission, together with personal vicissitudes within the Institute, drive the Servant of God to strengthen and further mature her abandonment of faith through its expression in unceasing prayer, as a frequent recourse to God full of trust. In this second stage one can observe the maturing of faith in the exercise of hope.

Finally, evident are those elements that confine the experience of faith within the bounds of union with God and the Church, elements hardly describable except through phenomenological indicators that can only approximate their meaning while nonetheless showing their authenticity. More manifest in this period is the theme of charity in the Servant of God's works and expressions, accompanied by a gradual giving of herself to the point of exhaustion, and by repeated but restrained references to victory over the devil, assurances of healings, dreams, forebodings and prophecies.

c) The Virtues

The virtue that best illustrates the exercise of the Servant of God's spiritual gifts, and on which all the other inner and outer dispositions wrought in her by grace solidly rest, is certainly humility. There is no portion of her writings in which the coherence and consistency of this fundamental condition does not show through. It is visible especially from a twofold perspective, the inner and the outer.

Inwardly, this virtue acts as a disposition toward perfection in awareness of the limits of her own nature, that is, in a situation of constant dependence on the grace of God, which alone can fill what is lacking in her own inadequacy. It generates an unconditional readiness to cooperate with God, so that his will for good and his power of salvation may be manifested in others. What is astonishing in all this is how, even in the inner dimension, this desire for self-improvement is outward-facing, that is, oriented to the ultimate good of others at the expense of her own interest. Generally lacking is any reference to a personal quest for, or cultivation of, perfection as an end in itself. The only hint in this direction, though not in an individualistic sense but with a view to her mission, can be read in her declaration of total readiness to let Christ educate her soul through correction.

Outwardly, the Servant of God's extreme humility takes shape in the uninterrupted exercise of an absolute and undivided obedience to the rule and to the superiors of the Institute, especially to the foundress, toward whom she nurtures and cultivates a special veneration. Obedience rooted in humility lends genuineness to the expressive fabric that shapes her epistolary communications in a style typical of the time, and restores it in its spiritual integrity, free, that is, from any stylistic — and therefore psychological — dissonance that might unduly surface for a contemporary reader accustomed to a different style. Obedience is lived as the royal road to the realization and enjoyment of communion. It calls upon and engages the wholly personal dimension of the individual, who thus manifests the fundamental love of the rule, as an explication of the evangelical path to salvation; devotion to superiors as representatives of the visibility and care of God and of Jesus Christ; the full assumption of entrusted duties and the need to be answerable for them to the end, as a response to the call to holiness; the seeking of counsel and guidance, as openness to the Spirit's illumination; readiness for correction through self-accusation and penance, as a confident affirmation of docility to God's design upon the person and upon circumstances.

Conclusion

The considerations drawn up for this opinion are based entirely on a close reading of the material examined. Each of them translates and organizes in a synthetic perspective the very affirmations found in the contents of the letters. The result, as can be seen, is a thoroughly positive opinion on the object, together with a particular admiration for the work that God himself accomplished in and through Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi.

In all conscience, before God, I can affirm that I have taken every care to report whether there is anything in the writings of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi contrary to the faith and to good morals, and I reaffirm that I have found nothing contrary to the faith and to good morals.

Palermo, 13 April 1999

In witness whereof.

Prof. Rosario La Delfa

2. Opinion of the Most Reverend Prof. Don Antonino Raspanti, second theological Censor of the writings of the Servant of God, dated 13 April 1999 (Proc. pp. 440-442).

A reading of the letters of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi which were given to me reveals no element that could be, or sound, contrary to the faith and/or the Christian morals professed by the Catholic Church. And although they do not furnish many elements that directly reveal the inner life of the Servant of God, they do allow her spiritual physiognomy to be sketched with sufficient assurance.

In her rigorous and scrupulous reporting to the Foundress, or to her fellow sisters, of the conditions of the communities and of their work, the traits of her personality lie hidden. Through her constancy in the practice of the virtues and in discharging the duties of her state with the responsibilities entrusted to her, the Servant of God shows to what degree she had assimilated the spirit of the Institute, in her minute observance of the Rule and her unconditional obedience to the Foundress and to her direct superiors. Her evident eagerness to live out that spirit, above all in caring for the sick and in fidelity to the Rule, up to within a few days of her death, though already gravely ill, shows the heroic endurance of this woman, who tirelessly sought to obey and thereby to follow the divine will.

This regularity, lived out with a serene and benevolent bearing toward everyone, has its unmistakable source in her personal relationship with the Lord, which now and then peeks through in the letters. From her youth she knew a taste for prayer, which became the inexhaustible wellspring of her life, to the point of being unable to resist the Lord and finding no further consolation in this world. Prayer grows with her, taking on the color of the various needs and the various seasons of the Servant of God's life, but it is always an expression of total availability and full trust in God's provident intervention in her own life, in that of the Institute, of those she cares for, and of those who turn to her in any need. The many difficulties and trials she encountered were all borne and resolved in long periods of adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, which instilled in her courage and optimism; these feelings she passed on to her correspondents, managing to let any negative feeling, or even mere discouragement, die completely within her.

This full rootedness in God through prayer not only gave her strength in fulfilling her duties, but gave her the impetus of an unshakeable obedience, founded on humility. Among all the Christian virtues she practiced, these two stand out and account for the choices made at the main turning points of her life: her entry into the Institute, the day after her transfer from Florence, and her fervent work in Sicily. Firmly rooted in her is the conviction that God's will is manifested and followed by obeying the Foundress and the Rule, awaiting from her superiors the necessary correction. She never shows full confidence in her own judgment or conduct, but always submits everything to the Foundress's judgment, and never shows negative feelings toward her fellow sisters, who, moreover, perceive the sincerity and loyalty of her words, to the point of admiring her. She does not therefore consider that she should ever oppose even certain unjust accusations against her, but recalls instead the meek and calm obedience of Isaac, who offered himself in sacrifice. The absence, in the letters, of lengthy considerations and digressions about the state of her soul cannot cast doubt on the high degree of perfection she attained; on the contrary, taken together with the testimony of her tireless self-giving to others to the point of exhausting her strength, it consistently shows how she arrived at the ultimate consequences of humility and obedience, living in full self-concealment and self-forgetfulness. The Servant of God is found wholly in the actions carried out in perfect charity, documented in the laconic statements about the running of the houses she directed.

In conclusion, from an attentive reading of the material I can express a positive opinion on the object, expressing admiration and gratitude for the work of God accomplished in the Servant of God and for the generous and heroic readiness she showed.

Antonino Raspanti

B. Assessment of the Sources for the Purposes of the Process

The list of archives consulted and the indication of the documentation found, particularly that preserved in the Historical Archive of the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne, show that an investigation has been carried out which may be considered sufficient for the purposes of preparing the Positio super virtutibus and for the judgment of the historical and theological consultors and of the Most Eminent Cardinals.

I. Life of the Servant of God

From the documents there emerges a clear and straightforward human and spiritual story of the Servant of God, which can be divided into two major phases:

- the first may be dated from her birth (22 February 1842) to her entry into the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne: this is the period of her human formation and growth in faith, of assiduous labor and generous service to her family, both to her many younger siblings and to close relatives, such as the priest uncles with whom she lived for some time;

- the second phase runs from her entry into the newborn Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne (4 November 1868) to her death (7 June 1885): this is the period of rapid Christian maturation, marked by an ardent love for Jesus the bridegroom that drove her to follow him more closely along the path of the evangelical counsels, in solicitous devotion to the sick and to her fellow sisters, in continuous prayer.

As for the first phase, the documents let us know about the family setting and her early progress in spiritual life. The Servant of God "was a young woman of good character — Luigi Curà attests — of a gentle disposition, of a great heart [...] sincere, cheerful, modest"; she was inclined to piety and mortification; she helped her mother raise her younger siblings not only with material care but also by passing on the religious teachings she herself was learning and then pondering in prayer. For some time she was in service to two priest uncles, showing kindness and wisdom in running their respective rectories; she also lovingly looked after and cared for two brothers who attended the Seminary of Bedonia as day students. In her youth she was for some time inclined toward marriage, but she later felt called to consecrate herself to God in the service of her neighbor, and she did so with resolve and determination.

As for the second phase, the documents allow us to follow the Servant of God's intense activity as a home-visiting nurse in various communities in Italy: first at Sampierdarena, then at Genoa, and then at Sestri Ponente, winning the admiration of her fellow sisters: "Even from then on — Sister Anna Paolina Viani affirms — the sisters spoke of the exemplary conduct of this good sister, conduct which, however, had nothing unusual about it. One admired in her a great humility, obedience, charity toward all, scrupulous exactness in fulfilling her duties, in observance of the holy rule; in short, she was greatly edifying."

Her work as a nurse brought out her capacity to care for those who suffered, among whom she always chose the poorest and those afflicted with repugnant illnesses, as Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi attests: "She loved the poor as the very person of Jesus; indeed she preferred the poorest and neediest, consoling them with such sweetness that she always left them content." From her youth she affirmed that prayer was the only consolation she had in this world, and on this path she steadily progressed.

Very soon the Foundress, Venerable Anna Rosa Gattorno, entrusted her with the office of superior, and Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi carried it out with great wisdom, humility and charity, never abandoning her care of the sick. We thus find the Servant of God in 1874 at San Martinello (Perugia) and in 1875 in Florence. In this city she encountered difficulties because of the lack of understanding and the hostility of the Archbishop's Delegate for religious, Canon Luigi Ciaranfi, who felt he should interfere in the internal running of the Institute. Sister Anna del Salvatore, in keeping with the Foundress's directives, did not permit such interference, which risked distorting the Institute's purpose.

For reasons of prudence, the Foundress transferred her in April 1878 to Appignano (Macerata) as superior of that community. Subsequently, however, during the spiritual exercises at Piacenza in August of that same year, for the Institute's superiors, the Foundress — under pressure from negative assessments by some of the superiors — decided to send her to Ferrara without any leadership role. It was a moment of great trial for the Servant of God, who was almost held responsible for what had happened in Florence. From the documents, and in particular from the testimony of Sister Anna Costanza Cenni, it can be inferred that the possibility of dismissing her from the Institute was even considered. The Servant of God faced it all with humble serenity and great strength of spirit, submitting herself completely to the Foundress's judgment.

Soon the situation was clarified and the atmosphere calmed, and the Servant of God was sent, at the end of that same year 1878, to lead the community of Via dei Riari in Rome. She was then sent to Sermoneta, then to Ovada, and finally to the city of Palermo as superior, to open the community of home-visiting nurses. She also held the office of Provincial Superior for Sicily, contributing notably to the Institute's expansion on the island, in a historical period of growing pauperism and also of sharp conflict between the Church and the State authorities. She was greatly esteemed by the people and clergy of Palermo, in particular by Cardinal Michelangelo Celesia, who sought her out for counsel.

These brief notes show how the Servant of God, in her life, constantly sought God's will and let herself be led by it, renouncing her own plans and trustingly committing herself to the Lord in every circumstance, joyful or sorrowful. Her constant characteristic was assiduous prayer and generous charity toward her brothers and sisters, favoring the most suffering and the least, after the example of the Savior and drawing inspiration from St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate Mary.

II. Spiritual Physiognomy of the Servant of God

From the documents gathered, the figure of the Servant of God clearly emerges, not only in the chain of events of her historical course, but also in her particular spiritual physiognomy.

Sister Anna del Salvatore was a shining example of faithful following of the Lord and of generous, limitless charity toward others, because in her life she gave herself entirely to the Lord, let herself be guided and shaped by him, growing continually in the knowledge of Jesus and in love for him, and continually broadening her capacity for concrete and effective self-giving.

The characteristic traits of her spirituality, as can be gathered from the documents, are well summarized by the Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne, Venerable Anna Rosa Gattorno, in her letter of June 1886, in which, together with the General Council, she asks the Cardinal Archbishop of Palermo, Michelangelo Celesia, for the canonical recognition of the Servant of God's mortal remains: "The heroic virtues exercised by the Servant of God within and outside the religious house, accompanied by a humility at once simple and profound, with an impenetrable spirit of self-concealment:

The spirit of prayer and union with God, which raised her to the highest contemplation.

The spirit of most severe penance, with which she sacrificed herself to her God.

The ready and tireless charity in attending to the sick of every kind.

The kindness toward her fellow sisters, for whom she always had a mother's tender heart."

We can sketch the spiritual physiognomy of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi by following precisely this line suggested by one who had occasion to know her very well over the years.

The spirit of prayer is the most genuine expression of faith. Faith led the Servant of God to adhere to her Lord and to seek an ever fuller communion with him. From the documents and testimonies it emerges that her whole life was a continuous dialogue with the divine Persons of the Holy Trinity. And it was this constant prayer that made her ready to do God's will in the various circumstances of her life. It likewise made her assume an inward attitude of great trust in God's provident and loving intervention in everyday life.

Her relationship with God, learned within her natural family and within the parish family of which she felt an active member, became ever more personal and intimate. "She devoutly attended the holy sacraments — the parish priest Don Tommaso Grilli attests — she devoutly said her prayers; at novenas or feasts, even devotional ones, she would come to attend them." And Don Giuseppe Giacopazzi relates that her mother "found her up at night praying when she was still very small."

Having entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, she continued to progress along this path. Sister Anna Maristella Calderone says of her: "The chief thought and affection around which the whole life and activity of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore gathered was nothing other than God. Of him she spoke continually with her fellow religious sisters, of him she reasoned with the sick she went to care for, on his perfections she meditated, of him she felt the continuous presence... Her very actions were interpenetrated with prayer, which from lip or heart never ceased."

Other fellow sisters likewise unanimously attest to her continuous prayer: she prayed at the bedside of the sick when not occupied in serving them; she spent every free moment of the day before the Blessed Sacrament, and very often whole nights, or a great part of them; in prayer, often, especially after making her Holy Communion, she remained absorbed, to the point of not noticing what was happening around her. Her words made it clear how her thoughts were constantly absorbed in God. "She spoke of her Beloved with such tenderness — Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte affirms — that she would inflame even the hardest hearts."

In every problem or need of her own, of the Community, of the Institute, of people in general, she had recourse with great trust to prayer, and was often heard. In the house in Florence, for example, finding herself in financial straits, she writes to the Foundress: "Jesus will provide, because he is my treasurer... yesterday the bread bill came to me: I began to laugh because I had only 30 francs and the bill came to almost 90 francs, but the Lord, so good, provided me with that and then even more..." (16 March 1877). Sister Anna Maristella Calderone attests: "She asked trustingly to obtain, and with the confidence that only love can give, endless graces and favors for all who were in need, and how many graces her faith obtained!"

The Foundress herself, Venerable Anna Rosa Gattorno, relied on her prayers, as emerges from many testimonies and can be inferred from the Servant of God's own letters. She writes to the Foundress on 19 January 1884: "I hope the Lady Countess [Carlotta Custo Barbiellini, the Foundress's daughter] will soon be consoled... Yes, Mother, good God will grant her the grace, always, however, through dear little Mother Mary, most certain that she will obtain it...".

The Servant of God's so luminous faith was accompanied by a lively sense of humility.

This virtue places the person in her truth as a creature before God, in the condition of receiving everything from him as a gift, and is an expression of inner poverty. Sister Anna del Salvatore truly followed Jesus' teaching: "Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart," and always sought self-concealment.

In the obituary that appeared in "La Sicilia Cattolica" of 12 June 1885, we read: "She was such that merely approaching her, one found oneself captivated as if by enchantment, not knowing what to admire first in her — her profound humility or her dignified bearing; the sweetness of her manner or the sobriety of her dealings; the strength of a lion or the meekness of a lamb...".

The low opinion she held of herself led her to treat people with gentleness, in particular her fellow sisters, in whom she was always ready to recognize merits and virtues. Writing to the Foundress, she often notes at the close of her letters: "the sisters are all well, cheerful and content"; "the sisters are well and good"; "the sisters too are all well, and all at peace, which is truly a pleasure."

Her letters are all permeated with feelings of humility. As superior, she fears making mistakes that might harm her fellow sisters and the Institute; she therefore submits all her conduct to the Foundress, and is even ready to give up the office of superior. "I hope everything will go well — she writes on 22 December 1875 — if you believe me; but if you do not trust me, my good mother, believe me that I do everything I can... but if I haven't enough ability...".

When she believes she has erred, she humbly asks forgiveness and requests that a penance be assigned to her. She writes on 24 May 1880: "Reverend Mother, here I am prostrate at your maternal feet, with tears in my eyes, I accuse myself guilty of a grave fault committed yesterday [...] for this fault committed by me I ask your maternal heart for forgiveness and for penance, resolved never again to commit such faults [...] always, however, by divine help [...]".

She fled from praise, and if she received any she was ready to disclose what she thought of herself, and everything good that was in her she attributed to the mercy of God and the goodness of others. On 17 February 1885 she answers Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega, who had used words of praise toward her: "It is only through the great mercy of good God and the very great goodness of our dear Mother that I have been brought to this point, of being able to live in community, and through the goodness of the sisters who so charitably bear with me; for the rest I am nothing but an abyss of iniquity...".

Her deep humility led the Servant of God to bear with serenity being accused unjustly, and to refrain from defending herself, seeking her defense in God alone. Although her conscience reproached her with nothing, she asks forgiveness for the grief she caused involuntarily, and faced with possible dismissal from the Institute, confides to Sister Anna Costanza Cenni: "I will offer no resistance at all; I will do as Isaac did, who made the sacrifice of his life. I will lay my head on the Mother's knees, as Isaac laid himself on the bundle of wood; let her do as she wishes, I will offer no resistance, but if I must leave the Institute I will try to do as much good as I can for the Institute".

Faith and an intense relationship with God necessarily lead to oblative love for one's neighbor. The commandment of love, which Jesus indicated as the greatest, together with love of God, and as a sign by which the world might believe, was lived by Sister Anna del Salvatore with particular overtones toward her fellow sisters and the people she was called by vocation to care for. Love of neighbor sprang from her awareness of being loved by God, an awareness that filled her with inner joy; she thus placed herself beside people with attitudes of a typically maternal devotion, drawing her inspiration from Mother St. Anne.

As a simple sister and as superior, the feelings of esteem and benevolence she bore toward her fellow sisters led her to be attentive to their needs and to anticipate them, showing on every occasion a truly maternal delicacy. During the night watches at the bedsides of the sick she took upon herself the heaviest part, as Sister Anna Paolina Viani attests: "Toward us, too, who had been given to her as companions and helpers, she showed great charity and wanted us to rest, especially when there was no great need for both of us to be attending her at once; she, however, was tireless and never wanted to rest, and when the patient did not need continuous care, in those intervals she would pray".

She sought in every way to ease the burden on her fellow sisters, doing the heaviest household chores herself. Sister Anna Gregoria Poppelmann affirms: "[She was] all heart and charity toward those under her, whom she loved as a tender mother, and she knew how to draw honey even from bitter flowers. And what shall we say of her charity toward the sick sisters? They were her favorite portion". And she continues: "She would go to keep vigil in a home visit, and when it was her turn to rest, she would spend the night pumping water, washing linens, and making flowers for the chapel...".

She always showed particular devotion in caring for the sick, among whom she preferred the poorest and neediest. Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte attests: "Immense was the charity she had for the poor and abandoned sick, especially those with contagious diseases. The Servant of God attended them with love and charity, cleaned them, dressed their putrid and gangrenous sores, exhorted them to have patience and resignation, and had them regard their bed as the Cross of Jesus; she had them go to confession, receive Communion, and prepared them for the great passage".

Sister Anna Nazaria Provera likewise affirms: "She was solicitous toward the poor sick, spending whole nights lavishing on them all the care their infirmities required. She sweetened their suffering with the most gracious manner, to such a degree that word spread that she was a great saint. All the sick wished to be cared for by her, for the relief they felt".

Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari highlights the deep motivations of her charity: "The poor! They were indeed the person of Christ for our heroine; on them she lavished all her care with the fervor of one who wishes to please her beloved; to them her pure and comforting smiles, to them the caresses and the cheerful help that never humiliated, and all flocked to her, both the needy and the afflicted... For the sick she had, moreover, a vocation of love: to them she gave her labor with the devotion of one who senses the good, sublimates it, makes it beautiful".

The Servant of God's spiritual physiognomy also includes — as the Foundress's letter to Cardinal Celesia quoted above attests — a marked spirit of penance. From her youth she had grasped the value of asceticism in the Christian life as a means of purification, of sharing the condition of the poor, of identification with the Crucified Christ, and she never neglected it.

"With praiseworthy patience she bore the lack of things she often needed," the parish priest of Albareto, Don Tommaso Grilli, relates of her. And Orsolina Bottego attests that "to make a sacrifice of her life she ate almost always only vegetables."

Having entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, the Servant of God led a life of great penance. She took only one meal a day and even suffered some humiliation for being faithful to this choice. Sister Anna Guida witnessed this: "In the two and a half months we were together in Ferrara [1878] I saw her suffer mistreatment at table, especially once, but she never complained and kept up her practice of eating only once a day. It seems to me that sometimes she was made to have supper, and that she obeyed." Sister Anna Raffaela Ceruti attests that the Servant of God "was most mortified in her eating, contenting herself most of the time with eating the sisters' leftovers, doing this with such ease as not to be noticed by the community"; and Sister Anna Paolina Viani confirms: "She would cover up her mortification by saying that her stomach could not retain delicate food, and that, on the contrary, it was those poor scraps that suited her stomach; one was left in admiration of her mortification and her humility in hiding her penances."

Sister Anna del Salvatore also used instruments of penance, hairshirts and the discipline, as attested, among other fellow sisters, by Sister Anna Letizia Sordi, who had seen them herself: "However much she tried to hide it, we could tell that getting up and sitting down caused her a good deal of pain"; "Before the doctor arrived [to see her], a hairshirt fell to the floor, and was picked up by a sister, to her great distress." Sister Anna Consolata Massimelli affirms that "at night she slept very little; in the biting cold of Ovada she kept her window open while praying." Sister Anna Leonilde heard her using the discipline on herself, having happened to pass through a corridor.

What struck her fellow sisters greatly was the fact that the Servant of God had given up having her own room and bed. "Her abstinence from food — Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari relates — was matched by her abstinence from sleep: she had no bed, her place of rest being the holy tabernacle." Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte confirms: "She allowed her body very little sleep, spending whole nights praying on her knees or seeing to some task to relieve the sisters, or else going to tend the sick in their homes."

Most significant is what the Servant of God writes to the Foundress, Venerable Anna Rosa Gattorno, on 28 February 1884: "I hear you tell me to rest at least four hours. Yes, my Mother, I am most ready and have already done so at once... Ah! my Mother, what sorrow... yes, what sharp sorrow I feel; I see in this a severe punishment for my sins, and perhaps, indeed without perhaps, for the little profit I made of them...".

III. Continuity of the Reputation for Sanctity

From the documents it is evident that already in her lifetime the Servant of God enjoyed a reputation as a highly virtuous person, heroic in the practice of every virtue. The love of God burning within her radiated upon all who came near her.

Sister Anna del Consiglio Chiaramonte affirms: "Although the Servant of God was so modest and reserved in her conduct, attributing to God the merit of working miracles, people, edified by such rare modesty, held her in such high esteem that they called her a saint. People of every class and condition flocked to her for advice and instruction and to receive heavenly graces and favors."

"Of Sister Anna del Salvatore's reputation for sanctity — Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari confirms — the echo still resounds in Palermo: whoever knew her truly loved her, as the saints are loved and venerated, and even today, when I happen to speak of her with someone who admired her virtues up close, I feel the pride of belonging to the Family of a 'sweet saint,' as they called her, a saint in feeling and in word."

Her reputation for sanctity did not die out with her death, but on the contrary grew ever stronger. The documents reveal the interest in her life, the veneration aroused by the various examinations of her mortal remains, and the memory of her that lives on in her native town, Albareto, where the Nursery School bears her name.

In the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne the echo of her virtues, and the hope that her sanctity would be recognized, never died away, and this led to the request made by the Chapter Assembly of 1984 to reopen the Cause of beatification of Sister Anna del Salvatore.

Conclusion

In presenting this report to Your Most Reverend Eminence, we declare that we take responsibility for all that is set forth in it.

We consider that the documentation gathered is sufficient to assess the path of sanctity of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi and the efficacy of her witness in the Church of her time, as well as its value and meaning for the Church today, without, however, presuming to pronounce a judgment that is reserved to the Congregation for the Causes of Saints alone.

The documentation indeed comprises the writings, almost entirely autograph, of the Servant of God, and numerous other texts concerning the events of her life. From them one can reconstruct her service of charity and her spiritual journey.

Grateful for the task entrusted to us, which we believe we have carried out with diligence, we offer our respectful regards.
